123. SPI^{\ast }: Uniform weak ultrafilter principle: For each family F of infinite sets \exists f such that \forall x \in F, f(x) is a non-principal ultrafilter on x. Halpern [1972]

143. H(C,TR): If (X,\,R) is a connected relation (u\neq v\rightarrow u\,R\,v\ \mathrm{or}\ v\,R\,u) then X contains a \subseteq -maximal transitive subset. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

201. Linking Axiom for Boolean Algebras: Every Boolean algebra has a maximal linked system. (L \subseteq B is linked if a \wedge b\neq 0 for all a and b\in L.) Schrijver [1978].

[201 A] Strong Linking Axiom for Boolean Algebras: Each linked system in a Boolean algebra is contained in some maximal linked system. (If B is a Boolean algebra, L\subseteq B is linked if a\wedge b\neq 0 for all a and b\in L.) Schrijver [1978].

[202 A] H(TR\&C,P): If (X,\,R) is a transitive, connected relation. Then X has a \subseteq -maximal partially ordered subset. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

206. The existence of a non-principal ultrafilter: There exists an infinite set X and a non-principal ultrafilter on X. Blass [1977b].

225. Every proper filter on \omega can be extended to an ultrafilter. Rav [1977].

244. Every principal ideal domain has a maximal ideal. Hodges [1976a] and note 84.

254. Z(D, P, l): Every directed relation (P, R) in which ramified subsets have least upper bounds, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

255. Z(D, R): Every directed relation (P,\,R) in which every ramified subset A has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

256. Z(P,F): Every partially ordered set (X,\,R) in which every forest A has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

257. Z(TR,\,P): Every transitive relation (X,\,R) in which every partially ordered subset has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

258. Z(D,\,L): Every directed relation (X,\,R) in which linearly ordered subsets have upper bounds, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

259. Z(TR\&C, W): If (X,\,R) is a transitive and connected relation in which every well ordered subset has an upper bound, then (X,\,R) has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

260. Z(TR\&C,P): If (X,\,R) is a transitive and connected relation in which every partially ordered subset has an upper bound, then (X,\,R) has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

261. Z(TR,\,T): Every transitive relation (X,\,R) in which every subset which is a tree has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

262. Z(TR,\,R): Every transitive relation (X, R) in which every ramified subset A has an upper bound, has a maximal element. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

263. H(AS\&C,P): Every every relation (X,\,R) which is antisymmetric and connected contains a \subseteq -maximal partially ordered subset. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

264. H(C, P): Every connected relation (X,\,R) contains a \subseteq -maximal partially ordered set. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

265. H(A,\,TR): Every relation (X,\,R) contains a \subseteq -maximal transitive subset. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

266. H(AS,\,P): Every antisymmetric relation contains \subseteq -maximal partially ordered subset. Harper/Rubin [1976] and note 39.

278. In an integral domain R, if every ideal is finitely generated then R has a maximal proper ideal. Hodges [1974] and note 45 E.

289. If S is a set of subsets of a countable set and S is closed under chain unions, then S has a \subseteq -maximal element. Smullyan [1994] and note 102.

303. If B is a Boolean algebra, S\subseteq B and S is closed under \wedge , then there is a \subseteq -maximal proper ideal I of B such that I \cap S =\{0\}. H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985].

308(p). If p is a prime and if \{G_{y}:y\in Y\} is a set of finite groups, then the weak direct product \prod _{y\in Y}G_{y} has a maximal p-subgroup. Howard/Yorke [1987] and note 24.

[308 A(p)] If p is a prime and if Y is a set of non-empty, finite sets, then the weak direct product \prod _{y\in Y}S_{y} has a maximal p-subgroup. (S_{y} is the symmetric group on y.) Howard/Yorke [1987] and note 24.

[317 A] If B is a complete, well orderable Boolean algebra and A is a Boolean algebra of which B is a subalgebra, then there is an ideal I of A satisfying I\cap B =\{0\} and I is maximal among those ideals J of A satisfying J\cap B=\{0\}. Howard [1973].

345. Rasiowa-Sikorski Axiom: If (B,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a Boolean algebra, a is a non-zero element of B, and \{X_{n}:n\in \omega \} is a denumerable set of subsets of B then there is a maximal prime filter F of B such that a\in F and for each n\in \omega , if X_{n}\subseteq F and \bigwedge X_{n} exists then \bigwedge X_{n}\in F. Morillon [1988].

MEASURES (FORMS INVOLVING MEASURES ON SETS)

[14 AV] Every Boolean algebra has a 2-valued measure. Pincus [1972c] and note 147.

[14 BC] If m_{0} is an additive, real valued measure on a subalgebra \mathcal{B}_{0} of a Boolean algebra \mathcal{B} then there exists a measure m on \mathcal{B} such that m=m_{0} on \mathcal{B}_{0} and the range of m is contained in the closure of the range of m_{0}. Tarski [1930] and note 147.

37. Lebesgue measure is countably additive. Sierpiński [1916].

[52 A] On every Boolean algebra there is an additive real valued measure. Luxemburg [1969] and note 147.

[52 B] For every proper filter \mathcal{F} of elements of a Boolean algebra \mathcal{B}, there exists an additive, real valued measure m on \mathcal{B} such that m(x)=1 for all x\in \mathcal{F}. Luxemburg [1969] and note 147.

[52 C] For every non-empty set X and every proper ideal \mathcal{I} of in \mathcal{P}(X) there is a measure m on \mathcal{P}(X) such that m(x)=0 for all x\in \mathcal{I}. Luxemburg [1969] and note 147.

[52 D] Let \mathcal{B}_{0} be a subalgebra of a Boolean algebra \mathcal{B} and m_{0} an additive, real valued measure on \mathcal{B}_{0}. Then there is a real valued, additive measure m on \mathcal{B} such that m=m_{0} on \mathcal{B}_{0} and the range of m is contained in the closed convex hull of the range of m_{0}. Luxemburg [1969] and note 147.

[70 C] There is a 2-valued measure on \mathcal{P}(\omega ). Pincus [1972c] and note 147.

93. There is a non-measurable subset of \mathbb{R}. Sierpiński [1918].

221. For all infinite X, there is a non-principal measure on \mathcal{P}(X). Pincus/Solovay [1977] and note 147.

222. There is a non-principal measure on \mathcal{P}(\omega ). Pincus/Solovay [1977] and note 147.

223. There is an infinite set X and a non-principal measure on \mathcal{P}(X). Pincus/Solovay [1977] and note 147.

310. The Measure Extension Theorem: Suppose that \mathcal{A}_{0} is a subring (that is, a,\,b\in \mathcal{A}_{0}\rightarrow a\vee b\in \mathcal{A}_{0} and a-b\in \mathcal{A}_{0}) of a Boolean algebra \mathcal{A} and \mu is a measure on \mathcal{A}_{0} (that is, \mu \,:\,\mathcal{A}\rightarrow [0,\,\infty ],\,\mu (a\vee b)=\mu (a)+\mu (b) for a\wedge b=0, and \mu (0)=0.) then there is a measure on \mathcal{A} that extends \mu . Wagon [1985].

311. Abelian groups are amenable. (G is amenable if there is a finitely additive measure \mu on \mathcal{P}(G) such that \mu (G)=1 and \forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu (gA)=\mu (A).) Wagon bib:1985u.

312. A subgroup of an amenable group is amenable. (G is amenable if there is a finitely additive measure \mu on \mathcal{P}(G) such that \mu (G)=1 and \forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu (gA)=\mu (A).) Wagon [1985].

313. \mathbb{Z} (the set of integers under addition) is amenable. (G is amenable if there is a finitely additive measure \mu on \mathcal{P}(G) such that \mu (G)=1 and \forall A\subseteq G,\,\forall g\in G,\,\mu (gA)=\mu (A).) Wagon [1985].

[370 A] Measured Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem: If \mathcal{B} is a Boolean algebra and there is a measure on \mathcal{B} then there is an ultrafilter on \mathcal{B}. Morillon [1989], [1990] and note 147.

(Y\subseteq X is a transversal for \mathcal{U} if for all y\in \mathcal{U},\, y\cap Y\neq \emptyset .) Schrijver [1978].

[14 AT] Assume D and E are sets and for all d\in D,\,d is finite. Suppose that for every finite F\subseteq D, there is an S such that (\forall f\in F)(f\cap \,S\in E). Then there is an S such that (\forall d\in D)(d\cap \,S\in E). van Benthem [1975].

[14 BB] Fraïssé’s Theorem: Let \mathcal{E} be inductively ordered (that is, for any E,\,E^{\prime }\in \mathcal{E},\,\exists E^{\prime \prime }\in \mathcal{E} such that E\cup E^{\prime }\subseteq E^{\prime \prime }.) For any E\in \mathcal{E}, assume \mathcal{R}_{E} is a finite set of m-ary relations on E. If for any E,\,E^{\prime }\in \mathcal{E} with E\subseteq E^{\prime } we have \forall R\in \mathcal{R}_{E^{\prime }},\,R/E\in \mathcal{R}_{E} then there is an m-ary relation S on \bigcup \mathcal{E} such that S|E\in \mathcal{R}_{E} for any E\in \mathcal{E}. Bénéjam [1970]. See [14 Y].

[14 CF] A projective limit of a directed projective system of non-empty sets is non-empty. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

17. Ramsey’s Theorem I: If A is an infinite set and the family of all 2 element subsets of A is partitioned into 2 sets X and Y, then there is an infinite subset B\subseteq A such that all 2 element subsets of B belong to X or all 2 element subsets of B belong to Y. (Also, see form 325.) Jech [1973b] p 164 prob 11.20 and Ramsey [1929].

[34 A] \exists \alpha <\omega _{2} such that there are no hereditarily countable sets of rank \alpha . Jech [1982] and note 48.

[43 I] Form [106 A] + form 10. Blass [1979].

[43 P] The ultraproduct of a well founded structure by a countably complete ultrafilter is well founded. Spector [1980] and note 54.

[88 A] P(2,2): If X is a set and P is a property of subsets of X of 2 character (that is, \forall y\subseteq X(P(y)\ \mathrm{iff}\,\forall z\subseteq y(|z|\leq 2\rightarrow P(z)))) then if every finite subset of X can be partitioned into two or fewer P-sets (that is, sets z such that P(z)) then X can be partitioned into two or fewer P-sets. Cowen [1982].

[126 F] Every denumerable family of sets having the sfip also has a pseudo-intersection. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[132 A] Every set mapping f:X\rightarrow [X]^{WO} (well orderable subsets of X) on a Dedekind finite, infinite set X has an infinite free subset. Brunner [1989]. notes 22 and 94.

137(k). Suppose k\in \omega -\{0\}. If f is a 1-1 map from k\times X into k\times Y then there are partitions X=\bigcup _{i<k}X_{i} and Y=\bigcup _{i<k}Y_{i} of X and Y such that f maps \bigcup _{i<k}(\{i\}\times X_{i})\ \mathrm{onto}\ \bigcup _{i<k}(\{i\}\times Y_{i}). Truss [1984].

[137 A(k)] For all X and Y\subseteq \mathbb{R} form 137(k) holds. Truss [1984]

138(k). Suppose k\in \omega . If f is a partial map from k\times Y onto k\times X (that is, the domain is a subset of k\times Y), then there are partitions X= \bigcup _{i<k}X_{i} and Y=\bigcup _{i<k}Y_{i} of X and Y such that f maps \bigcup _{i<k}(\{i\}\times Y_{i}) onto \bigcup _{i<k}(\{i\}\times X_{i}). Truss [1984].

[138 A(k)] For all standard X and Y, form 138(k) holds. Truss [1984]. This is equivalent to 138(k) in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

[140 A] (Form 137 with k=2): If f is a 1-1 map from 2\times X into 2\times Y then there are partitions X=X_{0}\cup X_{1} and Y=Y_{0}\cup Y_{1} of X and Y such that f maps (\{0\}\times X_{0})\cup (\{1\}\times X_{1}) onto (\{0\}\times Y_{0})\cup (\{1\}\times Y_{1}). Truss [1984].

152. D_{\aleph _{0}}: Every non-well-orderable set is the union of a pairwise disjoint, well orderable family of denumerable sets. Brunner/Howard [1992]. (See note 27 for D_{\kappa },\,\kappa a well ordered cardinal.)

172. For every infinite set S, if S is hereditarily countable (that is, every y\in TC(S) is countable) then |TC(S)|=\aleph _{0}. Jech [1982].

179(\epsilon ). Suppose \epsilon >0 is an ordinal. \forall x,\,x\in W(\epsilon ). David [1980] and note 25.

184. Existence of a double uniformization: For all X and Y, for all E\subseteq X\times Y, if there is an infinite cardinal \kappa satisfying:

(1)

\forall y_{0}\in Y,\,|\{(x,\,y_{0}):x\in X\}\cap E|=\kappa and

(2)

\forall x_{0}\in X,\,|\{(x_{0},\,y):y\in Y\}\cap E|=\kappa ,

then \exists U\subseteq E such that for all (x,\,y)\in E,\,\exists !z\in X such that (z,\,y)\in U and \exists !z\in Y such that (x,\,z)\in U. (U is called a double uniformization of E.) Kaniewski/Rogers [1980].

191. SVC: There is a set S such that for every set a, there is an ordinal \alpha and a function from S\times \alpha onto a. Blass [1979].

192. EP sets: For every set A there is a projective set X and a function from X onto A. Blass [1979] and note 60.

[201 B] Disjoint Transversal axiom (2,2): If X is a set and \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V} are subsets of \{y\subseteq X:|y|\leq 2\} and if for each two finite subsets \mathcal{U}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V}_{0}\subseteq \mathcal{V} there are transversals Y_{1} and Y_{2} for \mathcal{U}_{0} and \mathcal{V}_{0} respectively such that Y_{1}\cap Y_{2}=\emptyset , then there are disjoint transversals X_{1} and X_{2} for \mathcal{U} and \mathcal{V} respectively (Y\subseteq X is a transversal for \mathcal{U} if for all y\in CalU,\, y\cap Y\neq \emptyset .) Schrijver [1978].

230. L^{1}=HOD. Szczepaniak [1977] and note 82.

234. There is a non-Ramsey set: There is a set A of infinite subsets of \omega such that for every infinite subset N of \omega ,\,N has a subset which is in A and a subset which is not in A. Prikry [1976] and Mathias [1968].

282. \omega {\not \rightarrow } (\omega )^{\omega }. Erdös/Rado [1952], Kleinberg/Seiferas [1973] and note 97.

309. The Banach-Tarski Paradox: There are three finite partitions \{P_{1},\,\ldots ,\,P_{n}\},\,\{Q_{1},\, \ldots ,\,Q_{r}\} and \{S_{1},\,\ldots ,\,S_{n},\,T_{1},\,\ldots ,\,T_{r}\} of B^{3}=\{x\in \mathbb{R}^{3}:|x|\leq 1\} such that P_{i} is congruent to S_{i} for 1\leq i\leq n and Q_{i} is congruent to T_{i} for 1\leq i\leq r. Banach/Tarski [1924].

325. Ramsey’s Theorem II: \forall n,\,m\in \omega , if A is an infinite set and the family of all m element subsets of A is partitioned into n sets S_{j},\,1\leq j\leq n, then there is an infinite subset B\subseteq A such that all m element subsets of B belong to the same S_{j}. (Also, see form 17.) Ramsey [1929].

ORDERING PRINCIPLES INCLUDING PROPERTIES OF PARTIAL ORDERS

I. Linear And Well Orderings

[\boldsymbol{0} Z] Suppose X and M are sets, F is a function from \mathcal{P}(X)-\{\emptyset \} into M and G is a function on M such that \forall z\in \mathcal{P}(X)-\{\emptyset \},\,G(F(z))\in \mathcal{P}(z)-\{\emptyset \}. Then there are unique W and R such that W\subseteq M,\,R\subseteq W\times W and R is an irreflexive well ordering of W, the range of G|W is a partition of X, and \forall w\in W,\,w=F(X-\,(\bigcup \{G(\nu )\,:\nu \in W\,\mathrm{and}\,\nu \,R\,w\})). Kruse [1974].

[\boldsymbol{0} AH] No infinite well orderable set is amorphous.

[1 J] Form 49 + form 51. Morris [1969] and note 121.

[1 K] Form 133 + form 64. Clear

[8 G] Let R be a relation and R^{\ast }, the transitive closure of R. (x\,R^{\ast }\,y iff there exists a finite ascending R-chain connecting x to y.) If every ascending R-chain is finite, then every ascending R^{\ast }-chain is finite. Diener [1994].

[15 B] SDO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is a dense linear ordering of y. Pincus [1997].

[15 C] SUO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is an unbounded linear ordering of y. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus [1997].

[15 D] SDUO: For any family X of infinite sets, there is a function f with domain X such that \forall y\in X,\,f(y) is a dense unbounded linear ordering of y. Pincus [1997].

30. Ordering Principle: Every set can be linearly ordered. Schröder [1988].

[30 A] If R is a partial ordering in which the set of predecessors of each element is linearly ordered, then there is a linear ordering extending R. Felgner [1969].

[30 B] ADO: Every infinite set differs finitely from a set with a dense linear ordering: for all infinite x, there is a y\subseteq x such that y has a dense linear ordering and x-y is finite. Pincus [1997].

[30 C] SADO: For every set F there is a function f with domain F such that for all x\in F,\, f(x)\subseteq x,\,f(x) has a dense linear ordering, and x-f(x) is finite, Pincus [1997].

[30 D] UO: There exists an unbounded linear ordering on every infinite set. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus [1997].

[30 E] ADUO: For all infinite x, there exists y\subseteq x such that y has a dense unbounded linear ordering and x-y is finite. Pincus [1997].

[30 F] SADUO: For every set F there is a function f with domain F such that for all x\in F,\, f(x)\subseteq x,\,f(x) has a dense unbounded linear ordering, and x-f(x) is finite. Pincus [1997].

49. Order Extension Principle: Every partial ordering can be extended to a linear ordering. Tarski [1924] p 78.

51. Cofinality Principle: Every linear ordering has a cofinal sub well ordering. Sierpiński [1918] p 117.

[51 A] For all linear orders (X,\,\leq ), there is a sup function on the bounded, well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[51 C] For every linearly ordered set (X,\,\leq ), if every well ordered subset of X is bounded above then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[67 B] MW: Each set can be covered by a well ordered family of finite sets. Levy [1962].

77. A linear ordering of a set P is a well ordering if and only if P has no infinite descending sequences. Jech [1973b] p 23.

[77 A] If a linearly ordered set (X,\,\leq ) has no greatest element then it has a subset of order type \omega . Sierpiński [1918].

79. \mathbb{R} can be well ordered. Hilbert [1900] p 263.

90. LW: Every linearly ordered set can be well ordered. Jech [1973b] p 133 and Felgner/Jech [1973].

91. PW: The power set of a well ordered set can be well ordered. Jech [1973b] p 133 and H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985].

103. If (P,\,<) is a linear ordering and |P|>\aleph _{1} then some initial segment of P is uncountable. Jech [1973b] p 164 prob 11.21.

[118 G] Each complete linear order admits an extreme choice, that is, if (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order then there is a choice function f on the set of non-empty open interval of X with the property that for all (a,\,b,\,c)\in X^{3} with a<b<c,\,f((a,\,c))\in \{f((a,\,b)),\,b,\,f((b,\,c))\}. Morillon [1991a].

[118 H] For each linear order (X,\,\leq ), there is an ordinal \alpha and a strictly increasing injective map j from (X,\,\leq ) to \{0,1\}^{\alpha } with the lexicographic order. Morillon [1987].

[118 I] Every linearly ordered set of linear orders each of which is non-empty and conditionally complete has a choice function. Morillon [1988], van Douwen [1985], and note 71.

[118 J] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear, complete order, then the order topology on X is hereditarily normal. Morillon [1988], van Douwen [1985], and note 71.

[118 K] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is highly separated. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 L] If X is a linear, complete order, then the order topology on X is highly separated. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 M] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the family \{A(a,\,b):a,\,b\in X\wedge a<b\} has a choice function. (A(a,\,b) denotes the set of continuous, order preserving functions from X into [0,1] such that f(a)=0 and f(b)=1.) Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 N] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the family \{A^{\prime }(a,\,b):a,\,b\in X\wedge a<b\} has a choice function. (A^{\prime }(a,\,b) denotes the set of continuous functions from X into [0,1] such that f(a)=0 and f(b)=1.) Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 O] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is effectively normal. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 P] If (X,\,\leq ) is a complete linear order, then the order topology on X is effectively normal. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 Q] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is hereditarily normal. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 R] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is monotonely normal. Morillon [1987] and note 71.

[118 S] If (X,\,\leq ) is a complete linear order, then there is a choice function \ast for the family of non-empty open intervals of X such that if a,\,b,\,c\in X and either (a,\,b)\neq \emptyset or (b,\, c)\neq \emptyset , then \ast ((a,\,c))\in \{\ast ((a,\,b)),\,\ast ((b,\,c)),\,b,\,b^{+}\} (where b^{+} is the successor of b if it exists and b otherwise). Morillon [1987] and note 71.

[118 T] Every complete linear order has an increasing choice function. Morillon [1987] and note 71.

129. For every infinite set A,\,A admits a partition into sets of order type \omega ^{\ast }+\omega . (For every infinite A, there is a set \{\langle C_{j},\,<j\rangle :j\in J\} such that \{C_{j}:j\in J\} is a partition of A and for each j\in J, <j is an ordering of C_{j} of type \omega ^{\ast }+\omega .) Brunner [1984f].

130. \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}) is well orderable. Brunner [1984f].

133. Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset. Brunner [1982a].

163. Every non-well-orderable set has an infinite, Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [1982a] and note 94.

164. Every non-well-orderable set has an infinite subset with a Dedekind finite power set. Brunner [1982a], notes 42 and 94.

[170 B] There is an uncountable, well orderable set of reals. Raisonnier [1982] and note 3.

185. Every linearly ordered Dedekind finite set is finite. Hickman [1979a] and note 94.

[185 A] If X is a linearly ordered set and there is neither an increasing nor a decreasing injection f:\omega \rightarrow X, then X is finite. Hickman [1979a].

198. For every set S, if the only linearly orderable subsets of S are the finite subsets of S, then either S is finite or S has an amorphous subset. Hickman [1978b] and note 57.

227. For all groups G, if every finite subgroup of G can be fully ordered then G can be fully ordered. Rav [1977] and note 79.

228. Every torsion free Abelian group can be fully ordered. Rav [1977] and note 79.

229. If (G,\,\circ ,\,\leq ) is a partially ordered group, then \leq can be extended to a linear order on G if and only if for every finite set \{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\}\subseteq G, with a_{i}\neq the identity for i=1 to n, the signs \epsilon _{1},\,\ldots ,\,\epsilon _{n}\,(\epsilon _{i}=\pm 1) can be chosen so that P\cap S(a_{1}^{\epsilon _{1}},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}^{\epsilon _{n}})=\emptyset (where S(b_{1},\,\ldots ,\, b_{n}) is the normal sub-semi-group of G generated by b_{1},\,\ldots ,\,b_{n} and P=\{g\in G:e\leq g\} where e is the identity of G.) Rav [1977].

[231 A] Every almost well orderable set (W-set) is well orderable. Note 25.

293. For all sets x and y, if x can be linearly ordered and there is a mapping of x onto y, then y can be linearly ordered.

294. Every linearly ordered W-set is well orderable. Morris [1969] and note 25.

295. DO: Every infinite set has a dense linear ordering. Gonzalez [1995a].

[295 A] DUO: Every infinite set has a dense unbounded linear ordering. (An ordering is unbounded if there is neither a least element nor a greatest element.) Pincus [1997].

316. If a linearly ordered set (A,\,\leq ) has the fixed point property then (A,\,\leq ) is complete. ((A,\,\leq ) has the fixed point property if every function f:A\rightarrow A satisfying (x\leq y\Rightarrow f(x)\leq f(y)) has a fixed point, and ((A,\,\leq ) is complete if every subset of A has a least upper bound.) Höft/Howard [1994].

377. Restricted Ordering Principle: For every infinite set X there is an infinite subset Y of X such that Y can be linearly ordered. De la Cruz/Di Prisco [1996].

II. Versions Of Martin’s Axiom

[\boldsymbol{0} S] If (P,\,\leq ) is a quasi-order such that P is non-empty, well orderable and every antichain is finite then there is a P-generic filter . Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[1 Z] If (P,\,\leq ) is a quasi-order and P\neq \emptyset and every antichain is finite, then there is a P generic filter which is well orderable. Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[8 F] Martin’s Axiom (\aleph _{0}): Whenever (P\leq ) is a non-empty, ccc quasi-order (ccc means every anti-chain is countable) and \mathcal{D} is a family of \leq \aleph _{0} dense subsets of P, then there is a \mathcal{D} generic filter G in P. Kunen [1980], Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[10 I] Assume (P,\,\leq ) is a partial order such that P is a denumerable union of finite sets and contains a non-empty subset Q relative to which depths are defined for all x\in \mathrm{P}. If all Q-strong antichains of P are finite then for each denumerable family \mathcal{D} of dense sets there is a \mathcal{D} generic filter. Shannon [1990] and note 47.

[43 C] Existence of a generic set: If \mathcal{D} is a denumerable collection of dense sets in a partial order (P,\,\leq ) then for all p\in P there is a \mathcal{D} generic G with p\in G. Goldblatt [1985] and note 47.

[43 D] If \mathcal{D} is a denumerable collection of dense subsets of a partial order (P,\,\leq ) then for all p\in P there is a sequence f:\omega \rightarrow P with f(0)=p and (\forall n\in \omega )(f(n)\geq f(n+1)) and range (f)\cap D\neq \emptyset for all D\in \mathcal{D}. Goldblatt [1985].

171. If (P,\,\leq ) is a partial order such that P is the denumerable union of finite sets and all antichains in P are finite then for each denumerable family \mathcal{D} of dense sets there is a \mathcal{D} generic filter. Shannon [1990] and note 47.

III. Trees

[10 F] König’s Lemma: Every \omega tree has an infinite chain. Pincus [1972c], note 21, and note 35.

[43 H] Every tree in which every element has at least one successor has a branch. Blass [1979] and note note 21.

[86 A(\alpha )] If (P,\,\leq ) is a tree of height \lambda \leq \aleph _{\alpha } which has fewer than \lambda branches of height <\lambda then one of the following holds for the upside down tree (P,\, \geq ):

(a)

There is a cardinal \mu <\lambda such that (P, \geq ) does not contain a strong antichain of cardinality \mu .

(b)

(P,\,\geq ) contains a strong antichain of cardinality \lambda .

(c)

(P,\,\geq ) contains a chain of cardinality \lambda .

Shannon [1992] and note 119.

[106 A] DMC: Dependent Multiple Choice: Every tree in which every element has at least one immediate successor has a subtree whose levels are finite and in which every element has at least one immediate successor. Blass [1979], Brunner [1983c], Fossy/Morillon [1995] and note 21.

216. Every infinite tree has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain. Pincus [1972a] and note 21.

249. If T is an infinite tree in which every element has exactly 2 immediate successors then T has an infinite branch. Truss [1975], note 87 and note 21.

IV. Other Partial Ordering Properties (See note 71.)

[\boldsymbol{0} J] Zermelo’s Fixed Point Theorem: For every partially ordered set (X,\,\leq ), if every well ordered subset has a least upper bound then every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988a], Zermelo [1908b] and Abian [1980].

[\boldsymbol{0} K] For all partially ordered sets (X,\,\leq ), if there is a sup function \sigma on the well ordered subsets of X then every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[\boldsymbol{0} L] Caristi’s Fixed Point Theorem: If (X,\,\rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi : X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering (x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho (x,\,y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)) every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t \leq f(t) has a fixed point. Caristi [1976], Manka [1988a], and note 38.

[1 Q] For any partial order (X,\,\leq ) there is a \sup function on the bounded (above), well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[1 R] For any partial order (X,\,\leq ) there is a \sup function on the bounded subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[1 S] For any partial order (X,\,\leq ) if every well ordered subset of X is bounded then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[1 T] For every directed partial order (X,\,\leq ) there is a sup function on the bounded, well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[1 U] For every directed partial order, if every well ordered subset of X is bounded above then there is a sup function on the well ordered subsets of X. Manka [1988a] and note 38.

[1 V] For every partially ordered set (X,\,\leq ), if every well ordered subset is bounded above then every function f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Manka [1988a] and Abian [1980].

[1 AJ] Let \mathcal{F} be a family of mappings of a poset (X,\,\leq ) into itself such that \forall f\in \mathcal{F},\,\forall x\in X,\,f(x)\leq x. If for some element e of X each chain in X containing e has a lower bound, then the family \mathcal{F} has a common fixed point. Kasahara [1976].

[14 W] Universal Subnet Theorem: Any net has a universal subnet. Schechter [1996a] and note 31.

[43 K] Let M be a non-empty set partially ordered by < without <-minimal elements. Then there is a subset C of M which is linearly ordered by < such that C has no <-minimal element. Note 146.

[43 L] Z_{\omega }: If every chain in a partially ordered set P is finite, then P contains a maximal element. Tarski [1948], Wolk [1983], and note 54.

[43 M] If (X,\,\rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi :X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering, (x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho (x,\,y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)), there is a maximal element. Brunner [1987a] and note 38.

[43 Q] Matrix(\omega ): For every atomless poset (P,\,\leq ) and every family D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} of dense open subsets of P, there exists a matrix C=\{C_{i}:i\in \omega \},\, |\bigcup C|=\omega of P for D. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[43 R] Any partial order (A,\,\leq ) with no infinite descending chains is well founded, (that is, for all X such that \emptyset \,\neq X\subseteq A,\,X has a minimal element.) Spector [1980] and note 54.

59(\leq ). If (A,\,\leq ) is a partial ordering that is not a well ordering, then there is no set B such that (B,\,\precsim ) (the usual injective cardinal ordering on B) is isomorphic to (A,\,\leq ). Mathias [1979] p 120.

[70 B] Weak Universal Net Theorem: There is a universal net in \omega which is not eventually constant. Schechter [1996a] and note 31.

[87 A(\alpha )] Z_{\aleph _{\alpha }}: Let P be a partially ordered set in which every well ordered chain has type <\aleph _{\alpha }. If every well ordered chain in P has an upper bound in P, then P contains a maximal element. Wolk [1983].

[87 B(\alpha )] Z_{\aleph _{\alpha }}^{\ast }: Let P be a well-founded partially ordered set, (that is, every chain in P is well ordered), in which every chain has type <\aleph _{\alpha }. If every chain in P has an upper bound in P, then P contains a maximal element. Wolk [1983].

89. Antichain Principle: Every partially ordered set has a maximal antichain. Jech [1973b] p 133 and Kurepa [1953].

105. There is a partially ordered set (A,\,\leq ) such that there is no set (B,\,\precsim ) (\precsim , the usual injective cardinal ordering) isomorphic to (A,\,\leq ). Forti/Honsell [1985] and Jech [1966c].

144. Every set is almost well orderable. Keisler [1970] and note 25.

217. Every infinite partially ordered set has either an infinite chain or an infinite antichain. Pincus [1972a].

TOPOLOGICAL FORMS (INCLUDING PROPERTIES OF \mathbb{R})

I. Baire Category Type Theorems (See note 28.)

[43 E] The Baire Category Theorem for Čech Complete-I Spaces: Every Čech complete space is Baire. Goldblatt [1985] and note 28.

[43 F] Baire Category Theorem for Sequentially Complete Metric Spaces: Every sequentially complete metric space is Baire. Blair [1977], Brunner [1983c], Goldblatt [1985], and note 28.

[43 J] Baire Category Theorem for Cantor Complete Metric Spaces: Every Cantor complete metric space is Baire. Brunner [1983c] and note 28.

[43 T] A sequentially complete metric space is not meager. Note 28.

[43 U] Baire Category Theorem for Filter Complete Metric Spaces: Every filter complete metric space is Baire, Morillon [1988] and note 28.

[43 V] Every convex-compact set in a Hausdorff topological vector space with a basis of convex open sets is Baire. Fossy/Morillon [1995] and note 23.

106. Baire Category Theorem for Compact Hausdorff Spaces: Every compact Hausdorff space is Baire. Goldblatt [1985], G. Moore [1982], and note 28.

[106 C] Every scattered compact space is a Baire space. Fossy/Morillon [1995] and note 28.

II. Product Theorems

[\boldsymbol{0} B] If X is finite then X^{\omega } is compact. Brunner [1984b].

[\boldsymbol{0} D] Products of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [1984b]

[\boldsymbol{0} E] The box product of a well ordered family of limited amorphous spaces is limited amorphous. (A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [1984b] and note 52.

[1 AY] For each \lambda \in \Lambda let S_{\lambda } be a subset of some topological space X_{\lambda }. Then \mathrm{cl}( \prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }S_{\lambda })=\prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }\ \mathrm{cl}\ (S_{\lambda }), where the first “\mathrm{cl}” is closure in the product topology and the second “\mathrm{cl}” is closure in X_{\lambda }. Schechter [1992].

[1 AZ] For each \lambda \in \Lambda , let X_{\lambda } be a complete uniform space. Then, the product \prod _{\lambda \in \Lambda }X_{\lambda } equipped with the product uniform structure, is also complete. (See, for example, Kelley [1955] pp 176ff for definitions.) Schechter [1992].

[10 B] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Countable Families of Finite T_{2} Spaces: The product of a countable family of finite T_{2} spaces is compact. Krom [1981].

[14 J] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Compact Hausdorff Spaces: The product of compact Hausdorff spaces is compact. (For many compactness theorems T, it is clear that [14 J] implies T implies [14 K].) Łoś/Ryll-Nardzewski [1954] and Rubin/Scott [1954].

[14 K] Compactness of the Generalized Cantor Space: \{0,1\}^{I} is compact for any I. (For many compactness theorems T, it is clear that [14 J] implies T implies [14 K].) Jech [1973b] p 28, prob 17 and Mycielski [1964].

[14 Z] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Families of Finite Spaces: If \{X_{i}:i\in I\} is a family of finite topological spaces, then \prod _{i\in I}X_{i} is compact. (Cleary [14 Z] implies [14 K] and is implied by [14 J].) Jech [1973b] p 28 prob 17, A.A. Lewis [1983], and Wolk [1967].

[14 AB] Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Sober Spaces: A product of compact, sober topological spaces is compact. Blass [1986], Johnstone [1984] and note 37.

[43 G] Form 106 + form 154. Brunner [1983c] [1984b].

[64 A] An amorphous power of a compact T_{2} space is compact. Brunner [1984b].

[64 B] Finite products of metric C spaces are C. (A space is C if each open covering has an amorphous refinement.) Brunner [1984b].

113. Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Countably Many Spaces: The product of a countable set of compact spaces is compact. Brunner [1985a].

115. The product of weakly Loeb T_{2} spaces is weakly Loeb. (See form 114 for the definition of weakly Loeb.) Brunner [1985a].

127. An amorphous power of a compact T_{2} space, which as a set is well orderable, is well orderable. Brunner [1984b].

134. If X is an infinite T_{1} space and X^{Y} is T_{5}, then Y is countable. (T_{5} is “hereditarily T_{4}”.) A. H. Stone [1948].

135. If X is a T_{2} space with at least two points and X^{Y} is hereditarily metacompact then Y is countable. (A space is metacompact if every open cover has an open point finite refinement. If B and B^{\prime } are covers of a space X, then B^{\prime } is a refinement of B if (\forall x\in B^{\prime })(\exists y\in B)(x\subseteq y). B is point finite if (\forall t\in X) there are only finitely many x\in B such that t\in x.) van Douwen [1980].

139. Using the discrete topology on 2,\, 2^{\mathcal{P}(\omega )} is compact. Truss [1984].

154. Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for Countably Many T_{2} Spaces: The product of countably many T_{2} compact spaces is compact. Brunner [1983c].

177. An infinite box product of regular T_{1} spaces, each of cardinality greater than 1, is neither first countable nor connected. Brunner [1981a], Knight [1964], and note 52.

332. A product of non-empty compact sober topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

343. A product of non-empty, compact T_{2} topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon [1988].

351. A countable product of metrizable spaces is metrizable. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

352. A countable product of second countable spaces is second countable. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

353. A countable product of first countable spaces is first countable. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

354. A countable product of separable T_{2} spaces is separable. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

III. General Topology

[\boldsymbol{0} C] Closed subspaces of limited amorphous spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is compact.) Brunner [1984b].

[\boldsymbol{0} M] A T_{1} topological space is Dedekind finite if and only if every subspace has a dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.

[\boldsymbol{0} N] If X and Y are topological spaces with dense Dedekind finite subsets so is X\times Y. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.

[1 O] A(D1,\,C): For every T_{2} topological space (X,\,T), if X is covered by a well ordered family of closed, discrete sets then each family U\subseteq T of pairwise disjoint sets is well ordered. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

[1 P] A(P): (Depends on P for P\in \{W1,\,W2,\,B1,\,L1,\,L2, S,\,C,\,H1,\,A1\}) Every T_{2} topological space has property P. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

[1 BF] (\mathrm{D}T_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is dense in X. (Y is dense in X if there is no non-empty open subset O\subseteq X such that O\cap Y=\emptyset .) McCarten [1988] and note 106.

[1 BG] (\mathrm{C}T_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is codense in X. (Y is codense in X if there is no non-empty closed subset C\subseteq X such that C\cap Y=\emptyset .) McCarten [1988] and note 106.

[1 BH] (\mathrm{T}T_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is thick in X. (Y is thick in X if there is no non-empty open and closed (clopen) subset H\subseteq X such that H\cap Y=\emptyset .) McCarten [1988] and note 106.

[1 BI] (MT_{0}): Every topological space has a maximal T_{0} subspace. Schnare [1968] and note 106.

[1 BL] Every family of closed sets in a T_{2} topological space includes a maximal subfamily with the finite intersection property. Keremedis [1996b] and H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], p 60, M14.

[1 BM] For every family \{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\} of T_{1} topological spaces, the box topology contains an element \prod _{i\in k}O_{i}, such that \emptyset \neq O_{i} and O_{i}\neq X_{i} for all i\in k. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 BN] For every family \{(X_{i},\,T_{i}):i\in k\} of disjoint T_{1} topological spaces, the free union contains an open set O such that \emptyset \neq O\cap X_{i} and O\cap X_{i}\neq X_{i} for all i\in k. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 BO] For every T_{1} topological space (X,\,T) and every base (subbase) B for X there exists a \subseteq -maximal cellular family Q\subseteq B. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 BP] For every dense in itself topological space (X,\,T) and every base B for X there exists a nest N included in B. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 BQ] For every dense in itself topological space (X,\,T) and every base B for X there exists a tower R included in B. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 BR] For every T_{2} space (X,\,T) and every subbase \mathcal{B} for X, if \mathcal{C} and \mathcal{D} are cellular families of X included in \mathcal{B}, then there is a cellular family \mathcal{E} \subseteq \mathcal{B} such that \mathcal{C} and \mathcal{D} are equipollent to subsets of \mathcal{E}. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 BW] If (X,\,T) is a T_{4} topological space and U=\{U_{i}:i\in K\},\,|U_{i}|\geq 2, is a locally finite family of open non-empty pairwise disjoint sets, then there is a continuous real valued function f on X which assumes at least two distinct values on each U_{i}. Keremedis [1995] and note 43.

[1 CB] For every infinite cardinal \kappa , if (X,\,T) is a T_{2} space having a base B such that no Q\subseteq B,\,|Q|<\kappa , is a tower, then for every family \mathcal{D}=\{D_{i}:i\in \kappa \} of dense open sets of X there is a filter F\subseteq T such that for every i\in \kappa there is a b\in F with b\subseteq D_{i}. Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[1 CF] If a topological space is cwH, then it is cwH(B) for every basis B. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[1 CG] The disjoint union of cwH spaces is cwH(B) for every basis B. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[1 CH] If a topological space is cwN, then it is cwH(B) for any basis B. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[8 C] Every \sigma -compact space is Lindelöf. Brunner [1982b] and note 43.

[8 D] Every \sigma -compact, locally compact T_{2} space is weakly Lindelöf. Brunner [1982b] and note 43.

[8 I] A disjoint union of a countable set of Lindelöf T_{2} spaces is Lindelöf. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[8 J] Hemicompact T_{2} spaces are Lindelöf. (A hemicompact space is a space (X,\,T) that can be written as a disjoint union \bigcup \{K_{n}:n\in \omega \} such that (i) each K_{n} is a compact set in X; (ii) K_{N}\subseteq K_{n+1} for all n\in \omega ; and (iii) for every compact set K in X, there is an n\in \omega such that K\subseteq K_{n}.) Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[8 K] Hemilindelöf T_{2} spaces are Lindelöf. (In [8 J], in the definition of hemicompact replace “compact” by “Lindelöf” to get the definition of hemilindelöf.) Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[8 L] Every second countable topological space is separable. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[8 N] DP: If (X,\,T) is a topological space having a countable \pi -base, then for every family D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} of dense open sets of X, there is a countable dense set S\subseteq X such that for all i\in \omega and for all but finitely many s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[8 O] DUCCC\ + form 131. DUCCC is “If X is a denumerable family of disjoint topological spaces each having the ccc property, then the disjoint union of the spaces in X has the ccc property.” (Y has the ccc property if every collection of disjoint open sets is countable.) Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[8 P] DUSS\ + form 131. DUSS is “The disjoint union of a denumerable family of separable topological spaces is separable.” Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[8 Q] DUSC\ + form 131. DUSC is “The disjoint union of a denumerable family of second countable topological spaces is second countable.” Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[8 R] SCDUL\ + form 131. SCDUL is “The denumerable disjoint union of second countable spaces is Lindelöf.” Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[10 H] \sigma -compact, paracompact T_{2} spaces are weakly Lindelöf. Brunner [1982b] and note 43.

[13 B] There is a separable topological space X and a set A\subseteq \mathbb{R} such that X^{A\times \omega } has no dense, Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.

[14 BY] For every topological space X, every proper ideal in the normed \mathbb{R}-algebra of continuous bounded functions from X into \mathbb{R} is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon [1988].

[14 CB] If X is a topological space and I is a proper ideal in the algebra of all bounded continuous functions from X to \mathbb{R} such that every function in I vanishes at at least one point of X, then I is contained in a maximal ideal. Morillon [1988].

[40 A] A(L2,\,L1): For every T_{2} topological space (X,\, T), if each open cover of X has a well ordered subcover, then each open cover has a well ordered refinement. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

[50 L] Form 301 + form 14. Bell [1988].

[67 A] A(A2,\,H2): For every T_{2} topological space (X,\,T) if (X,\,T) is A2, then (X,\,T) is hereditarily A2. ((X,\,T) is A2 means if U\subseteq T covers X then \exists f:X\rightarrow T such that for all x\in X,\,x\in f(x) and f” X refines U.) Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

[67 C] A(P): (Depends on P\in \{D1,\,B2,\,B3,\,H2,\,A2\}.) Every T_{2} topological space has property P. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

[67 G] For every T_{1} topological space (X,\,T) and every cellular family \mathcal{O}= \{O_{i}:i\in k\}\subseteq T-\{\emptyset \}, there is a closed discrete set \mathcal{I} such that for every i\in k,\, \mathcal{I}\cap O_{i}\neq \emptyset . Keremedis [1996b] and note 77.

[67 I] If (X,\,T) is a T_{4} topological space and U=\{U_{i}:i\in K\} is a family of non-empty open sets, then there is a family F=\{f_{i}:i\in K\} of non-negative, non-constant, continuous real valued functions on X such that each f_{i} vanishes on X-U_{i}. Keremedis [1995].

[67 J] If (X,\,T) is a T_{4} topological space and U=\{U_{i}:i\in K\} is a family of non-empty open sets, then there is a family V=\{V_{i}:i\in K\} of non-empty closed (compact) sets such that U_{i}\supseteq V_{i} for each i\in K. Keremedis [1995].

[67 K] DUN: The disjoint union of normal topological spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997a] and note 141.

[67 L] DUU: If C is a collection of pairwise disjoint topological spaces each of which satisfies Urysohn’s lemma, then the disjoint union of the spaces in C satisfies Urysohn’s lemma. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997a] and note 141.

[67 M] DUT: If C is a collection of pairwise disjoint topological spaces each of which satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem, then the disjoint union of the spaces in C satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem. Howard/ Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997a] and note 141.

[67 N] DUP: The disjoint union of paracompact spaces is paracompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[67 O] DUMET: The disjoint union of metacompact spaces is metacompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[67 P] DUPFCS: The disjoint union of PFCS spaces is PFCS. (X is a PFCS space iff every point finite open cover of X is shrinkable.) Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[67 Q] DUPN: The disjoint union of paracompact spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[67 R] DUcwH: The disjoint union of cwH spaces is cwH. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[67 S] DUcwN: The disjoint union of cwN spaces is cwN. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[67 T] DUcwNN: The disjoint union of cwN spaces is normal. Howard/ Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

78. Urysohn’s Lemma: If A and B are disjoint closed sets in a normal space S, then there is a continuous f:S\rightarrow [0,\,1] which is 1 everywhere in A and 0 everywhere in B. Urysohn [1925] pp 290-292.

[91 A] A(S,\,W1): For every T_{2} topological space (X,\,T) if X has a dense well ordered subset, then T is well ordered. (Clear) Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

[94 A] The discrete topology on \omega is Lindelöf. Brunner [1982d] and note 40.

[94 B] There is a Lindelöf space with a closed, discrete infinite subset. Brunner [1982d] and note 40.

114. Every A-bounded T_{2} topological space is weakly Loeb. (A-bounded means amorphous subsets are relatively compact. Weakly Loeb means the set of nonempty closed subsets has a multiple choice function.) Brunner [1985a].

[126 C] FSCB\ + form 131. FSCB is “Every separable first countable space (X,\,T) has a denumerable \pi -base.” Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[126 E] If (X,\,T) is a topological space, then for every family D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} of dense open sets of X, there is a countable dense set S\subseteq X such that for all i\in \omega and for all but finitely many s\in S,\,s\in D_{i}. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[126 G] DUN(\omega ): The countable disjoint union of normal topological spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997a] and note 141.

[126 H] DUU(\omega ): If C is a countable collection of pairwise disjoint topological spaces each of which satisfies Urysohn’s lemma, then the disjoint union of the spaces in C satisfies Urysohn’s lemma. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997a] and note 141.

[126 I] DUT(\omega ): If C is a countable collection of pairwise disjoint topological spaces each of which satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem, then the disjoint union of the spaces in C satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997a] and note 141.

[126 J] F_{\sigma } subsets of paracompact spaces are paracompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

[126 K] F_{\sigma } subsets of metacompact spaces are metacompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b] and note 141.

128. Aczel’s Realization Principle: On every infinite set there is a Hausdorff topology with an infinite set of non-isolated points. Brunner [1984f].

[144 A] Every p space is discrete. (A p space is a T_{2} space in which the intersection of any well orderable family of open sets is open). Brunner [1984c].

146. A(F,\,A1): For every T_{2} topological space (X,\,T), if X is a continuous finite to one image of an A1 space then (X,\,T) is an A1 space. ((X,\,T) is A1 means if U\subseteq T covers X then \exists f:X\rightarrow U such that (\forall x\in X)(x\in f(x)).) Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

147. A(D2): Every T_{2} topological space (X,\,T) can be covered by a well ordered family of discrete sets. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

148. A(W2,\,B1): For every T_{2} topological space (X,\,T), if X is well ordered, then X has a well ordered base. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

149. A(F): Every T_{2} topological space is a continuous, finite to one image of an A1 space. Brunner [1983d] and note 26.

301. Any continuous surjection between Boolean spaces has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell [1988] and note 114.

360. Every second countable topological space is Lindelöf. G. Moore [1982] p 236.

371. There is an infinite, compact, Hausdorff, extremally disconnected topological space. Morillon [1993] and note 114.

375. Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem: If (X,\,T) is a normal topological space, A is closed in X, and f:A\rightarrow [0,\,1] is continuous, then there exists a continuous function g:X\rightarrow [0,\, 1] which extends f. Urysohn [1924].

IV. Linearly Orderable Spaces

[34 B] \omega _{1} with the order topology is not paracompact. Good/Tree [1995] and note 107.

[34 C] \omega _{1} with the order topology has the property that every infinite subset has a limit point in \omega _{1}. Good/Tree [1995] and note 107.

[34 D] \omega _{1} with the order topology does not contain a countable discrete family of open subsets. Good/Tree [1995] and note 107.

[34 E] \omega _{1} with the order topology is not Lindelöf. Good/Tree [1995] and note 107.

118. Every linearly orderable topological space is normal. Birkhoff [1967] p 241.

[118 A] For each complete linear order, the set of non-empty convex subsets has a choice function, van Douwen [1985].

[118 B] For each complete linear order, each pairwise disjoint collection of non-empty, convex, open subsets has a choice function, van Douwen [1985].

[118 C] Every linearly orderable space is collectionwise normal. van Douwen [1985] and note 71.

[118 D] Every linearly orderable space is collectionwise Hausdorff. van Douwen [1985] and note 71.

[118 E] Every linearly orderable space satisfies Urysohn’s lemma, van Douwen [1985] and note 141.

[118 F] Every linearly orderable space satisfies the Tietze-Urysohn extension theorem, van Douwen [1985] and note 141.

[118 J] If (X,\,\leq ) is a complete linear order, then the order topology on X is hereditarily normal. Morillon [1988], van Douwen [1985], and note 71.

[118 K] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is highly separated. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 L] If (X,\,\leq ) is a complete linear order, then the order topology on X is highly separated. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 O] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is effectively normal. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[118 R] If (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order, then the order topology on X is monotonely normal. Morillon [1987] and note 71.

[118 U] Every linearly ordered space is monotonically normal. (A space, (X,\,<) is monotonically normal if there is an operator V which assigns to each x\in X and basic open neighborhood U of x a basic open neighborhood V(x,\,U) of x such that V(x,\,U) \cap V(x^{\prime },\,U^{\prime })\neq \emptyset implies x\in U^{\prime } or x^{\prime }\in U.) Good/Tree [1995].

336. \omega _{1} with the order topology is not paracompact. Good/Tree [1995] and note 43.

V. Compact Spaces

[\boldsymbol{0} O] A Lindelöf space with a dense, Dedekind finite subset is compact. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.

[\boldsymbol{0} P] A Lindelöf space with a Dedekind finite basis is compact. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.

[1 AO] Any continuous surjection between compact spaces, where the range space is Hausdorff, has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell [1988] and note 114.

[1 BV] If (X,\,T) is a T_{4} topological space and G=\{G_{i}:i\in K\},\,|G_{i}|\geq 2, is a locally finite family of compact sets with non-empty pairwise disjoint interiors, then there is a continuous real valued function f on X which assumes at least two distinct values on each G_{i}. Keremedis [1995] and note 43.

[8 H] A disjoint union of a countable set of compact T_{2} spaces is Lindelöf. Keremedis [1996d] and note 132.

[14 L] Stone-Čech Compactification Theorem: For every topological space X there is a pair (Y,\,j) such that Y is a compact topological space and j is a continuous surjection from X onto Y such that for all topological spaces Z such that Z is compact and completely regular and for all continuous f:X\rightarrow Z, there is a unique continuous h:Y\rightarrow Z such that f=h\circ j. Rubin/Scott [1954] and note 71.

[14 AA] Alexander’s Subbase Lemma: A topological space is compact if and only if there is a subbase S for the topology such that every cover by elements of S has a finite subcover. Kelley [1955] p 143, A.A. Lewis [1983], Wolk [1967], and note 34.

[14 AG] Topological Rado Lemma: Let \{T_{i}:i\in I\} be a family of compact Hausdorff spaces and suppose for each finite F\subseteq I, there is a set \Phi (F) of partial choice functions on I whose domains include F and such that (a) F_{1}\subseteq F_{2} implies \Phi (F_{2})\subseteq \Phi (F_{1}) and (b) the set \{\phi |F:\phi \in \Phi (F)\} is closed in \prod \{T_{i}:i\in F\} in the product topology. Then there is a choice function f on I satisfying for any finite F\subseteq I,\,\exists \phi \in \Phi (F) such that f and \phi coincide on F. Rav [1977].

[14 AH] Principle of Consistent Choices: Let \{T_{i}:i\in I\} be a family of compact Hausdorf spaces and suppose R is a symmetric binary relation defined for all pairs of elements belonging to distinct T_{i} and such that for all i\neq j in I, the set E(i,\,j)=\{(x,\,y):x\,R\,y\ \mathrm{and}\ x\in T_{i}\ \mathrm{and}\ y\in T_{j}\} is closed in T_{i}\times T_{j}. Furthermore suppose that for every finite subset F\subseteq I, with at least two elements, \exists \phi \in \prod \{T_{i}:i\in F\} such that \phi (i)\,R\,\phi (j) for all i\neq j in F. Then \exists f\in \prod \{T_{i}:i\in I\} such that f(i)\,R\,f(j) for all i\neq j in I. Rav [1977].

[14 CC] A projective limit of compact topological spaces is compact. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[14 CD] A projective limit of a directed projective system of compact topological spaces is compact. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[14 CE] A projective limit of a directed projective system of compact nonempty topological spaces is non-empty. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[14 CG] A projective limit of a directed projective system of finite sets is compact. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

[50 E] Form 14 + form 297. Banaschewski [1988] and Bell [1988].

[50 J] Form 299 + form 14. Bell [1988].

[50 K] Form 300 + form 14. Bell [1988].

[50 M] Form 302 + form 14. Bell [1988].

[64 C] C spaces are compact. (A space is a C space if each open covering has an amorphous refinement.) Brunner [1984b].

[67 H] Let (X,\,T) be a T_{4} topological space and let \{G_{i}:i\in K\} be a locally finite family of pairwise disjoint, non-empty, open subsets of X. Then there exists a continuous real valued function f:X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that for each i\in K,\,f vanishes on the boundary of G_{i} and f(x_{i})=1 for some x_{i}\in G_{i}. Keremedis [1995] and note 43.

[106 D] For every compact T_{2} space (X,\,T) and every family D=\{D_{i}:i\in \omega \} of dense open sets of X there is a regular filter base \mathcal{F}\subseteq T (that is, if F,\,G\in \mathcal{F}, then there exists Q\in \mathcal{F} such that \overline{Q}\subseteq F\cap G) such that \forall i\in \omega , for all but finitely many F\in \mathcal{F},\,\overline{F}\subset D_{i}. Fossy/Morillon [1995].

116. Every compact T_{2} space is weakly Loeb. (See form 114 for the definition of weakly Loeb.) Brunner [1985a].

125. There does not exist an infinite, compact connected p space. (A p space is a T_{2} space in which the intersection of any well orderable family of open sets is open.) Brunner [1984c].

145. Compact P_{0}-spaces are Dedekind finite. (A P_{0}-space is a topological space in which the intersection of a countable collection of open sets is open.) Brunner [1984c] and note 94.

155. LC: There are no non-trivial Läuchli continua. (A Läuchli continuum is a strongly connected continuum. Continuum \equiv compact, connected, Hausdorff space; and strongly connected \equiv every continuous real valued function is constant.) Brunner [1983a] and Läuchli [1962].

156. Theorem of Gelfand and Kolmogoroff: Two compact T_{2} spaces are homeomorphic if their rings of real valued continuous functions are isomorphic. Brunner [1983a] and Gelfand/Kolmogoroff [1939].

157. Theorem of Goodner: A compact T_{2} space is extremally disconnected (the closure of every open set is open) if and only if each non-empty subset of C(X) (set of continuous real valued functions on X) which is pointwise bounded, has a supremum. Goodner [1950].

[225 A] There exists a compact, extremally disconnected topological space having a Dedekind infinite set of clopen subsets. Morillon [1993], notes 94 and 114.

[225 B] There exists a compact, \sigma -extremally disconnected topological space having a Dedekind infinite set of clopen subsets. Morillon [1993], notes 94 and 114.

297. Extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces are projective in the category of all compact Hausdorff spaces. Banaschewski [1988], Bell [1988], notes 60 and 114.

298. Every compact Hausdorff space has a Gleason cover. Bell [1988], Gleason [1958], and note 114.

299. Any extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff space is projective in the category of Boolean topological spaces. Bell [1988], notes 60 and 114.

300. Any continuous surjection between extremally disconnected compact Hausdorff spaces has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell [1988] and note 114.

302. Any continuous surjection between compact Hausdorff spaces has an irreducible restriction to a closed subset of its domain. Bell [1988] and note 114.

304. There does not exist a T_{2} topological space X such that every infinite subset of X contains an infinite compact subset. Brunner [1985c].

331. If (X_{i})_{i\in I} is a family of compact non-empty topological spaces then there is a family (F_{i})_{i\in I} such that \forall i\in I,\,F_{i} is an irreducible closed subset of X_{i}. Morillon [1988] and note 71.

VI. Properties of \mathbb{R}

[\boldsymbol{0} AB] If X\subseteq \mathbb{R} is perfect, then |X|=2^{\aleph _{0}}. Truss [1974b] and note 28.

[\boldsymbol{0} AC] There are 2^{\aleph _{0}} perfect subsets of \mathbb{R}. Truss [1974b] and note 28.

[6 A] Every uncountable subset of \mathbb{R} contains a condensation point. G. Moore [1982] p 205 and 324, Sierpiński [1918].

[6 B] Every uncountable subset of \mathbb{R} has two condensation points. G. Moore [1982] p 205 and 324, Sierpiński [1918].

11. \mathbb{R} is hereditarily Lindelöf. Lindelöf [1905].

12. \mathbb{R} is Lindelöf. Young [1903].

13. Every Dedekind finite subset of \mathbb{R} is finite. G. Moore [1982] and note 94.

[13 A] \mathbb{R} has no dense Dedekind finite subset. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.

19. A real function is analytically representable if and only if it is in Baire’s classification. G. Moore [1982] (2.3.1).

35. The union of countably many meager subsets of \mathbb{R} is meager. (Meager sets are the same as sets of the first category.) Feferman/Levy [1963], Jech [1973b] p 7 prob 1.7, and note 28.

36. If A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n} and A \bigcap B is countable for every bounded B then A is countable. G. Moore [1982] p 36.

37. Lebesgue measure is countably additive. Sierpiński [1916].

38. \mathbb{R} is not the union of a countable family of countable sets. Feferman/Levy [1963] and note 3.

73. For every A\subseteq \mathbb{R} and x\in \mathbb{R} the following definitions are equivalent:

(1) x is in the closure of A iff every neighborhood of x intersects A.

(2) x is in the closure of A iff there is a sequence \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A such that \lim x_{n}=x. Jech [1973b] p 21.

[73 A] For all A\subseteq \mathbb{R},\,x\in A and f:A\rightarrow \mathbb{R} the following are equivalent:

(1) (\forall \epsilon >0)(\exists \delta >0)(\forall y\in A)(|y-x|<\delta implies |f(y)-f(x)|<\epsilon )

(2) Whenever \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A and \lim x_{n}=x then \lim f(x_{n})=f(x). Notes 4, 5 and 6.

[73 B] (\forall f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R})(\forall x\in \mathbb{R}) the following are equivalent:

(1) (\forall \epsilon >0)(\exists \delta >0)((\forall y\in \mathbb{R}\rangle (|y-x|<\delta \rightarrow |f(y)-f(x)|<\epsilon )

(2) Whenever \lim x_{n}=x, then \lim f(x_{n})=f(x). Note 10.

74. For every A\subseteq \mathbb{R} the following are equivalent:

(1) A is closed and bounded.

(2) Every sequence \{x_{n}\}\subseteq A has a convergent subsequence with limit in A. Jech [1973b] p 21.

79. \mathbb{R} can be well ordered. Hilbert [1900] p 263.

[79 A] C(\infty ,\,\infty ,\,\mathbb{R}): Every set whose elements are non-empty subsets of \mathbb{R} has a choice function. Schechter [1996a].

92. Every subset of \mathbb{R} is separable. Jech [1973b] p 142.

93. There is a non-measurable subset of \mathbb{R}. Sierpiński [1918].

130. \mathcal{P}(\mathbb{R}) is well orderable. Brunner [1984f].

[137 A(k)] For all X and Y\subseteq \mathbb{R} form 137(k) holds. Truss [1984].

142. \neg PB: There is a set of reals without the property of Baire. Jech [1973b] p 7 and note 28.

169. There is an uncountable subset of \mathbb{R} without a perfect subset. Banaschewski/Moore [1990], Bernstein [1908], and note 28.

[170 A] There is a function that assigns to each denumerable set D of reals a real number not in D. Sierpiński [1954].

[170 B] There is an uncountable, well orderable set of reals. Raisonnier [1982] and note 3.

197. \mathbb{R}^{2} is the union of three sets C with the property that for all x\in C there is a straight line L such that L\cap C=\{x\}. Davies [1978].

203. C(\mathrm{disjoint},\subseteq \mathbb{R}): Every partition of \mathcal{P}(w) into non-empty subsets has a choice function. Truss [1978].

211. DCR: Dependent Choice for Relations on \mathbb{R}: If R\subseteq \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{R} satisfies (\forall x\in \mathbb{R})(\exists y\in \mathbb{R})(x\ R\ y) then there is a sequence \langle x(n): n\in \omega \rangle of real numbers such that (\forall n\in \omega )(x(n)\,R\,x(n+1)). Mathias [1977a].

212. C(2^{\aleph _{0}},\,\subseteq \mathbb{R}): If R is a relation on \mathbb{R} such that for all x\in \mathbb{R}, there is a y\in \mathbb{R} such that x\,R\,y, then there is a function f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that for all x\in \mathbb{R},\,x\,R\,f(x). Mathias [1977a].

224. There is a partition of the real line into \aleph _{1} Borel sets \{B_{\alpha }:\alpha <\aleph _{1}\} such that for some \beta <\aleph _{1},\,\forall \alpha <\aleph _{1},\,B_{\alpha }\in G_{\beta }. (G_{\beta } for \beta <\aleph _{1} is defined by induction, G_{0}=\{A: A\ {\text{is an open subset of}}\ \mathbb{R}\} and for \beta >0,\,G_{\beta }=\{\bigcup _{i=0}^{\infty }A_{i}:(\forall i\in \omega )(\exists \xi <\beta )(A_{i}\in G_{\xi })\} if \beta is even and G_{\beta }=\{\bigcap _{i=0}^{\infty }A_{i}:(\forall i\in \omega )(\exists \xi <\beta )(A_{i}\in G_{\xi })\} if \beta is odd.) Stern [1979].

251. The additive groups (\mathbb{R},\,+) and (\mathbb{C},\,+) are isomorphic. Ash [1975].

252. The additive groups of \mathbb{Q} \oplus \mathbb{R} and \mathbb{R} are isomorphic. Ash [1975].

272. There is an X\subseteq \mathbb{R} such that neither X nor \mathbb{R} -X has a perfect subset. Truss [1974b] and note 28.

273. There is a subset of \mathbb{R} which is not Borel. Truss [1974b].

305. There are 2^{\aleph _{0}} Vitali equivalence classes. (Vitali equivalence classes are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation x\equiv y\leftrightarrow (\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q).). Kanovei [1991].

306. The set of Vitali equivalence classes is linearly orderable. (Vitali equivalence classes are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation x\equiv y\leftrightarrow (\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q).). Kanovei [1991].

307. If m is the cardinality of the set of Vitali equivalence classes, then H(m)= H(2^{\aleph _{0}}), where H is Hartogs aleph function and the Vitali equivalence classes are equivalence classes of the real numbers under the relation x\equiv y\leftrightarrow (\exists q\in \mathbb{Q})(x-y=q). Kanovei [1991].

309. The Banach-Tarski Paradox: There are three finite partitions \{P_{1},\,\ldots ,\,P_{n}\},\,\{Q_{1},\, \ldots ,\,Q_{r}\} and \{S_{1},\,\ldots ,\,S_{n},\,T_{1},\,\ldots ,\,T_{r}\} of B^{3}=\{x\in \mathbb{R}^{3}:|x|\leq 1\} such that P_{i} is congruent to S_{i} for 1\leq i\leq n and Q_{i} is congruent to T_{i} for 1\leq i\leq r. Banach/Tarski [1924].

361. In \mathbb{R}, the union of a denumerable number of analytic sets is analytic. G. Moore [1982], pp 181 and 325.

362. In \mathbb{R}, every Borel set is analytic. G. Moore [1982], pp 181 and 325.

363. There are exactly 2^{\aleph _{0}} Borel sets in \mathbb{R}. G. Moore [1982], p 325.

364. In \mathbb{R}, there is a measurable set that is not Borel. G. Moore [1982], p 325.

366. There is a discontinuous function f:\mathbb{R} \rightarrow \mathbb{R} such that for all real x and y,\,f(x+y)=f(x)+f(y). Hamel [1905].

367. There is a Hamel basis for \mathbb{R} as a vector space over \mathbb{Q}. Hamel [1905].

368. The set of all denumerable subsets of \mathbb{R} has power 2^{\aleph _{0}}. Sierpiński [1917].

369. If \mathbb{R} is partitioned into two sets, at least one of them has cardinality 2^{\aleph _{0}}. Luzin/Sierpiński [1917].

VII. Metric Spaces

[\boldsymbol{0} L] Caristi’s Fixed Point Theorem: If (X,\,\rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi :X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering (x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\, \rho (x,\,y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)) every f:X\rightarrow X satisfying \forall t\in X,\,t\leq f(t) has a fixed point. Caristi [1976], Manka [1988a], and note 38.

[\boldsymbol{0} AK] Every separable metric space is second countable.

[1 I] In every metric space (X,\,d) there is an \epsilon -lattice for some \epsilon >0 which is not a strict upper bound of d. Brunner [1984e] and note 17.

[1 BK] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,\,d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is pairwise disjoint. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997].

[1 CE] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,\,d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is discrete. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[10 G] For all metric spaces X and Y and continuous functions f from X onto Y such that f^{-1}(y) is finite for all y\in Y, if X has a dense Dedekind finite subset, then so does Y. Brunner [1982d] and note 94.

[43 F] Baire Category Theorem for Sequentially Complete Metric Spaces: Every sequentially complete metric space is Baire. Blair [1977], Brunner [1983c], Goldblatt [1985] and note 28.

[43 J] Baire Category Theorem for Cantor Complete Metric Spaces: Every Cantor complete metric space is Baire. Brunner [1983c] and note 28.

[43 M] If (X,\,\rho ) is a complete metric space and \phi :X\rightarrow \mathbb{R} is bounded above and upper semi-continuous then in the Brøndsted ordering, (x\leq y\,\mathrm{iff}\,\rho (x,\,y)\leq \phi (y)-\phi (x)), there is a maximal element. Brunner [1987a] and note 38.

[64 D] Metric C spaces are limited amorphous. (A space is C if every open covering has an amorphous refinement. A space is limited amorphous if each amorphous subset is relatively compact.) Brunner [1984b].

[67 U] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,\,d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is locally finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[67 V] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X, d) can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is point finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

75. Every subspace of a separable metric space is separable. Jech [1973b] p 21.

[76 A] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is locally countable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[76 B] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{U_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where \gamma is an ordinal and each U_{\alpha } is point countable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

173. MPL: Metric spaces are para-Lindelöf. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[173 A] MML: Metric spaces are meta-Lindelöf. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/ Stanley [1997] and note 141.

232. Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \sigma -point finite base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[232 A] Every metric space has a \gamma -point finite base, for some ordinal \gamma . Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[232 B] Every metric space has a \sigma -locally finite base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[232 C] Every metric space has a \gamma -locally finite base, for some ordinal \gamma . Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[232 D] Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \sigma -discrete base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[232 E] Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \gamma -discrete base, for some ordinal \gamma . Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[232 F] Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \sigma -disjoint base. Howard/Keremedis/ Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[232 G] Every metric space (X,\,d) has a \gamma -disjoint base for some ordinal \gamma . Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

280. There is a complete separable metric space with a subset which does not have the Baire property. Wright [1973] and note 28.

337. Every separable metric space is Lindelöf. Good/Tree [1995].

338. Every second countable metric space is Lindelöf. Good/Tree [1995].

339. Every second countable metric space is separable. Good/Tree [1995].

340. Every Lindelöf metric space is separable. Good/Tree [1995].

341. Every Lindelöf metric space is second countable. Good/Tree [1995].

381. DUM: The disjoint union of metrizable spaces is metrizable. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b].

382. DUMN: The disjoint union of metrizable spaces is normal. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Rubin [1997b].

383. MP: Every metric space is paracompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[383 A] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X,\,d) has a refinement \mathcal{V} which covers X and which can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{V_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where each V_{\alpha } is locally finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[383 B] MM: Every metric space is metacompact. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.

[383 C] Every open cover \mathcal{U} of a metric space (X, d) has a refinement \mathcal{V} which covers X and which can be written as a well ordered union \bigcup \{V_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \gamma \} where each V_{\alpha } is point finite. Howard/Keremedis/Rubin/Stanley [1997] and note 141.
