NOTE 40

Notes on [94 A] and [94 B]. Brunner [1982d] proves that [94 B] implies form 13 (lemma 6, p. 164) by showing that the negation of form 13 implies the negation of [94 A] which implies the negation of [94 B]. Since [94 A] clearly implies [94 B], it only remains to prove that [94 A] implies 94 (to complete the argument for the equivalence of 94, [94 A] and [94 B]). (Form 94: C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ,\, \mathbb{R}); [94 A]: The discrete topology on \omega is Lindelöf; and [94 B]: There is a Lindelöf space with a closed, discrete infinite subset.)

Assume [94 A] and let \{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} be a denumerable family where for all i\in \omega ,\, A_{i}\neq \emptyset and A_{i}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\omega ). It suffices to find a choice function for the family \{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} (identifying reals with sets of natural numbers).

Now using the family \{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} we define a second family of sets of sets of natural numbers \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \} so that

\begin{equation*} \forall i\in \omega ,\, 2^{i}\in \bigcup B_{i}\ {\text{and for}}\ j\in \omega ,\,j\neq i\ {\text{implies}}\ 2^{i}\not \in \bigcup B_{j}. \tag{$\ast $} \end{equation*}

More specifically, for each i\in \omega , let m(i) be the least element of \bigcup A_{i}. Define f_{i}:\{k\in \omega :k\geq m(i)\}\rightarrow \omega by f_{i}(k)=[2(k-m(i))+1]2^{i} and let B_{i}=\{f_{i}^{\prime \prime }x:x\in A_{i}\}. It is clear that \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \} satisfies (\ast ) and that it suffices to find a choice function for \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \}. Further \bigcup _{i\in \omega }B_{i}\cup \big \{\{k\in \omega :k\not \in \bigcup _{i\in \omega }(\bigcup \,B_{i})\}\big \} is an open cover for \omega (using the discrete topology). Since the topology is Lindelöf there is a countable subcover \{x_{j}:j\in \omega \}. Defining, for each i\in \omega ,\,F(B_{i})=x_{j} where j is the least element of \omega such that 2^{i}\in x_{j} provides a choice function for \{B_{i}:i\in \omega \}.

NOTE 41

The following proof that form 233 is true in \mathcal{N}1 is due to David Pincus. Form 233 is “Algebraic closures of fields, if they exist, are unique.”

(H. Läuchli has given a proof of this lemma with the additional hypothesis that the characteristic of K is not equal to 2. See Jech [1973b], p. 147.)

Now let (K,\,+,\,\cdot ,\,0,1) be a field in \mathcal{N}1 with finite support E\subseteq A where A is the set of atoms. Assume that K is algebraically closed. We will show that every element of K has support E. This implies that all algebraically closed fields are well orderable in \mathcal{N}1 and therefore the standard proof of the uniqueness of algebraic closures (using AC) is valid in \mathcal{N}1.

The proof is by contradiction. Assume that x\in K does not have support E. We will arrive at a contradiction in two steps. The first is to show that for some permutation \pi of A which fixes E pointwise, \pi (x)\neq x and \pi ^{2} is the identity. The permutation \pi induces an automorphism of (K,\,+,\cdot ,\,0,1) and we can therefore apply the lemma to conclude that \pi (i)=-i\neq i for some square root i of -1 in K. The second step is to show that for every permutation \pi of A that fixes E pointwise, \pi (i)=i for every square root i of -1 in K.

For step one, suppose that x has support E\cup F where E\cap F=\emptyset . Let F^{\prime } be a subset of A for which |F^{\prime }|=|F| and F^{\prime }\cap (E\cup F)=\emptyset . Let \pi be a permutation of A which interchanges the elements of F and F^{\prime }, that is, \pi is a product of cycles of length 2, \pi =(a_{1},\,b_{1})(a_{2},\, b_{2})\cdots (a_{n},\,b_{n}) where F=\{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\} and F^{\prime }=\{b_{1},\,\ldots ,\,b_{n}\}. Clearly \pi ^{2} is the identity and \pi fixes E pointwise. The proof that \pi (x)\neq x is a standard permutation model argument and depends on the fact that x does not have support E.

For step two, we note that if i is a square root of –1 in K, then i is a solution to the equation x^{2}+1=0 all of whose coefficients are fixed by any permutation that fixes E pointwise. Therefore if \eta is a permutation of A that fixes E pointwise, \eta (i) is also a solution to x^{2}+1=0. Suppose that i does not have support E. Let E\cup F be a support of i where E\cap F=\emptyset . By a standard permutation model argument, we can show that if \pi and \pi ^{\prime } are any two permutations of A that fix E pointwise and \pi (F) \cap \pi ^{\prime }(F)=\emptyset then \pi (x)\neq \pi ^{\prime }(x). It follows that the equation x^{2}+1=0 has infinitely many solutions in K which is a contradiction and the proof is complete.

NOTE 42

In Brunner [1982a] is a study, in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} without AC, of conditions under which a topological space is well orderable. These conditions are summarized below.

Finally some counter examples: In the model \mathcal{M}1 (The basic Cohen model) X=[0,1] (the closed interval in \mathbb{R}) with the order topology is compact, metric, separable, second countable, hereditarily Souslin and linearly ordered, but X is not well orderable.

In the model \mathcal{N}3 (The ordered Mostowski model of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}): Let X=[a,\,b] be an interval in the set of atoms with the order topology. X is compact, hereditarily normal (that is T_{5}) and T_{2}. Further, each finite power of X is compact, T_{4} and hereditarily Souslin, but X is not well orderable.

In the model \mathcal{N}1 (The basic Fraenkel model with a denumerable set of atoms, using the group of all permutations of the atoms and finite supports): Let X= [A]^{<\omega } (all finite subsets of the set of atoms) with a basis for the topology all set of the form \{x:E\subseteq x and x\cap F=\emptyset \} where E and F range over the finite subsets of U. The space X is Souslin, perfectly regular and not well orderable.

NOTE 49

In von Rimscha [1982] three transitivity conditions are considered:

Tr.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f such that u is transitive and f is a function from f one to one and onto u. This is form 175.

Tr^{\prime }.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f such that u is transitive and u\subseteq TC(x) and f is a one to one function from x onto u.

Tr^{\prime \prime }.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f such that u is transitive and f is a one to one function from x onto u and \forall s\in x,\,f(s)\in TC(s).

It is shown that in ZF, AC implies Tr^{\prime \prime } and that Tr^{\prime \prime } implies Tr^{\prime } implies Tr. All proofs can be done in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} with minor modifications. It is also shown that \mathrm{ZF} \vdash Tr\rightarrow form 9 (Dedekind finite = finite). This could be reformulated as \mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash Tr\rightarrow all pure Dedekind finite sets are finite. We can therefore conclude that Tr (form 175) implies Dedekind finite sets of reals are finite (form 13).

It is however possible to prove in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} that Tr^{\prime \prime } (form 174) implies Dedekind finite = finite (form 9). We proceed as follows: Assume Tr^{\prime \prime }. We first show that every infinite subset of the atoms A is Dedekind infinite. Assume B\subseteq A and that B is infinite. We will use Tr^{\prime \prime } to get a choice function for \mathcal{P}(B) from which it follows that B has a denumerable subset. Let \kappa be the least well ordered cardinal which is not \leq |\mathcal{P}(B)|. For each a\in B and ordinal \alpha , define a_{\alpha } by induction: a_{0}=a,\,a_{\lambda }=\bigcup _{\alpha <\lambda }a_{\alpha } for limit ordinals \lambda and a_{\alpha +1}=a_{\alpha }\cup \{a_{\alpha }\}. (a_{\alpha } is the ordinal \alpha with every occurrence of \emptyset replaced by a.) Then for each \alpha ,\, |a_{\alpha }|=|\alpha |. Let B^{\prime }=\{a_{\kappa }:a\in B\} and let x=\mathcal{P}(B^{\prime }). By Tr^{\prime \prime } there is a transitive set u and a function f:x\rightarrow u which is one to one and onto and such that for each s\in x,\,f(s)\in TC(s). Suppose that C\subseteq B and let s=\{a_{\kappa }:a\in C\}\in x. Then

\begin{equation*} TC(s)=\{s\}\cup s\cup \bigg (\bigcup _{a\in C}a_{\kappa }\bigg ) \end{equation*}

since |TC(s)|\geq \kappa ,\,s\not \in u. (|u|=|\mathcal{P}(B)| which is not \geq \kappa .). So f(s)\in \bigcup _{a\in C}a_{\kappa }. Since a\neq b implies a_{\kappa }\cap b_{\kappa }=\emptyset ,\, f(s) determines a unique element of C.

Now let x be any infinite set. By Tr^{\prime \prime } there is a transitive u and a one to one function f from x onto u. If u contains only finitely many atoms, then the von Rimscha proof can be modified to show that x has a denumerable subset. If u contains an infinite set of atoms B, then by the first argument B and therefore x contains a denumerable subset.

Problem (from von Rimscha [1982]): Are any of the implications Tr\rightarrow Tr^{\prime }\rightarrow Tr^{\prime \prime }\rightarrow AC provable in ZF?

NOTE 57

Truss [1995] studies the various structures an amorphous set can carry. (A set is amorphous if it is infinite but is not the disjoint union of two infinite sets.) If \pi is a partition of an amorphous set U into infinitely many parts, then each part must be finite. (Otherwise, if X were an infinite part, then U=X\cup (U-X), contradicting the fact that U is amorphous.) Define a map f from U into \omega such that for each x\in U,\,f(x)=n where x\in \xi \in \pi and |\xi |=n. Since U is amorphous, the range of f must be finite. Since U=\bigcup \{f^{-1}(n): n\in range of f}, there is a unique n such that f^{-1}(n) is infinite. Let n(\pi ) be this unique n, then \{\xi \in \pi :|\xi |=n(\pi )\} is infinite.

Let \Pi (U) be the set of finitary partitions of U and let n(U)= \sup \{n(\pi ):\pi \in \Pi (U)\}. If n(U) is finite, U is called bounded, and if n(U) infinite, U is called unbounded.

NOTE 59

Form 191 is the statement: There is a set S such that for every set a, there is an ordinal \alpha and a function from S\times \alpha onto a and form 182 is: There is an aleph whose cofinality is greater than \aleph _{0}. In Blass [1979] it is proved, assuming form 191, that \forall A there is a limit ordinal \alpha such that A cannot be mapped cofinally onto \alpha . If A cannot be mapped cofinally onto \alpha , then A cannot be mapped cofinally onto \aleph _{\alpha }. Therefore form 191 implies form 182.

Blass also shows that if 191 holds with a set S then form 14 (the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem) holds if and only if there is an ultrafilter U on S^{<\omega } that is regular in the sense that \{p\in S^{<\omega }: s\in range p\} is in U for every s\in S.

With regard to (191,n), Blass shows that 191 holds in most known models of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} or ZF. In particular,

1.

Every permutation model whose class of atoms forms a set satisfies 191.

2.

Every symmetric model satisfies 191. (A symmetric model is a model constructed from a ground model M of ZFC by taking a complete Boolean algebra B in M, an M generic filter G in B, a group \mathcal{G} of automorphisms of B and a normal filter of subgroups of \mathcal{G}. The model consists of members of M[G] that have hereditarily symmetric names.)

3.

If V is any model of ZFC and A\in V, then the submodel HOD(A) of sets hereditarily ordinal definable over A satisfies 191.

NOTE 61

Kanovei [1979] studies the relationships between AC(K) and DC(K) where K is either in the analytic or projective hierarchy. We give definitions and summarize some of the results from Kanovei [1979]. AC(K) is: For any P\subseteq \omega \times {^{\omega }}\omega with domain \omega , if P\in K, then there is a sequence \langle x_{k}: k\in \omega \rangle of elements of {^{\omega }}\omega with \langle k,\,x_{k}\rangle \in P for all k\in \omega . And

DC(K) is: For every P\subseteq {^{\omega }}\omega \times {^{\omega }}\omega with domain ^{\omega }\omega , if P\in K then for any y\in {^{\omega }}\omega there is a sequence \langle x_{k}: k\in \omega \rangle with x_{0}=y and for all k\in \omega , \langle x_{k},\,x_{k+1}\rangle \in P. The sets in the analytic hierarchy (\varSigma _{n}^{1},\, \varPi _{n}^{1} and \varDelta _{n}^{1} for n\in \omega ) and the sets in the projective hierarchy (\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{n}^{1},\, \boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1} and \boldsymbol{\Delta }_{n}^{1} for n\in \omega ) are defined as follows: For purposes of these definitions ^{k,\ell }\omega is {^{k}}\omega \times {^{\ell }}(^{\omega }\omega ) and a relation R\subseteq {^{k,\ell }}\omega is of rank (k,\,\ell ).

1.

R of rank (k,\,\ell ) is arithmetic if for all \mathbf{m}\in {^{k}} \omega and all \boldsymbol{\alpha }\in {^{\ell }}(^{\omega }\omega ), R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }) iff Q_{1}x_{1}\ldots Q_{r}x_{r}P(\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },) where P\subseteq ^{r+k,\ell }\omega is recursive, and each Q_{i} is either \exists or \forall .

2.

R of rank (k,\,\ell ) is analytic if R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }) iff Q_{1}\beta _{1}\ldots Q_{r}\beta _{r}P(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\beta _{1},\,\ldots ,\,\beta _{r}) where P is of rank (k,\,\ell +r) and is arithmetic.

3.

(The analytic hierarchy)

(i)

\varSigma _{0}^{1}=\varPi _{0}^{1}= the arithmetic relations.

(ii)

\varSigma _{r+1}^{1}=\{\exists \beta P(\mathbf{m},\,\beta ,\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }):P\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}\wedge P has rank (k,\, \ell +1)\}

(ii)

\varPi _{n+1}^{1}=\{\forall \beta P(\mathbf{m},\,\beta ,\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }):P\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}\wedge P has rank (k,\, \ell +1)\}

(iv)

\varDelta _{r}^{1}=\varSigma _{r}^{1}\cap \varPi _{r}^{1}.

4.

R of rank (k,\,\ell ) is recursive in \boldsymbol{\beta } iff the characteristic function K_{R}(\mathbf{m},\, \boldsymbol{\alpha }) of R is G(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\boldsymbol{\beta }) for some partial recursive G.

5.

Assume \boldsymbol{\beta } has rank (0,\,\ell ) then \varSigma _{r}^{1}[\beta ] and \varPi _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }] are defined by R\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }] iff R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha })\leftrightarrow S(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\boldsymbol{\beta }) for some S\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}. \varPi _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }] is defined similarly.

6.

(The projective hierarchy)

(i)

\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{r}^{1}=\bigcup \{\varSigma _{r}^{1}[\beta ]:b\in {^{\omega }}\omega \}

(ii)

\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{r}^{1}=\bigcup \{\varPi _{r}^{1}[\beta ]:b\in {^{\omega }}\omega \}

(iii)

\boldsymbol{\Delta }_{r}^{1}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{r}^{1}\cap \boldsymbol{\Pi } 1_{r}.

In Kanovei [1979], it is shown for any n\geq 2 that, AC(\varPi _{n+1}^{1}) does not follow, in ZF from DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1}), that DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1}) implies AC(\varPi _{n}^{1}) and that AC(\varPi _{n}^{1}) does not imply DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1}). Kanovei [1976] has further results on AC and the projective hierarchy. See forms [0 X], 194 and 199.

NOTE 66

In this note we prove that form 322 (KW(WO,\,\infty )) is true in \mathcal{N}1. (Brunner [1982a], (Proposition 4.5) also has a proof of this result.)

Assume that X is a well ordered set in \mathcal{N}1 and that \forall y\in X,\,|y|\geq 2. Let E be a (finite) support of a well ordering of X and let fix(E) be the group of permutations of A (the set of atoms) which fix E pointwise. Then for all \phi \in fix(E), \phi fixes X pointwise. Choose an atom a\in A-E. We will show that for every y\in X,\,E\cup \{a\} is a support of a non-empty proper subset y^{\prime } of y. This will suffice since it follows that the function y\mapsto y^{\prime } is in \mathcal{N}1.

Choose an element y\in X. If every element of y has support E then any nonempty proper subset of y has support E and therefore has support E\cup \{a\}. So we may assume that y has some element t such that E is not a support of t. Choose a finite non-empty subset F of A such that E\cap F=\emptyset and E\cup F is a support of t and such that F is minimal in the sense that for no proper subset F^{\prime } of F is E\cup F^{\prime } a support of t. We may assume without loss of generality that a\in F. (If a\not \in F then we replace t by \psi (t) and F by \psi (F) where \psi is a permutation of A chosen so that \psi \in fix(E) and a\in \psi (F).) Let y'=\{\phi (t):\phi \in fix(E\cup \{a\})\}. Clearly y^{\prime } has support E\cup \{a\},\,y^{\prime }\subseteq y and y^{\prime }\neq \emptyset (since t\in y^{\prime }). It only remains to show that y^{\prime }\neq y.

Choose an \eta \in fix(E) so that \eta (F) \cap F=\emptyset . Then for every \phi \in fix(E\cup \{a\}), \eta (F)\neq \phi (F). It follows from the lemma that for all such \phi ,\,\eta (t)\neq \phi (t). Therefore \eta (t)\in (y-y^{\prime }).

NOTE 71

In this note we give definitions from Morillon [1988] for forms [14 L], [14 BP] through [14 BX], [14 CC] through [14 CH], [118 I] through [118 T], 331, 332, 343, 344, and [345 C] through [345 E].

Let X be a topological space, let E=\{(A,\,B):A and B are closed in X and A \cap B=\emptyset \} and let F=\{(U,\,V):U and V are open in X and U\cap V=\emptyset }.

1.

f:E\rightarrow F is a normality operator on X if \forall (A,\,B)\in E,\,f(A,\, B)=(U,\,V) where A\subseteq U and B\subseteq V.

2.

X is effectively normal if X is T_{2} and there is a normality operator on X.

3.

X is hereditarily normal (or completely normal) if all subspaces of X are normal.

4.

X is hereditarily effectively normal if all subspaces of X are effectively normal.

5.

A set I\subseteq \mathcal{P}(X) is discrete if \forall x\in X,\,\exists a neighborhood N of x such that N\cap A\neq \emptyset for at most one element A\in I.

6.

X is collectionwise normal if X is T_{2} and for every discrete I\subseteq \{U:U is closed in S\} there is a set J of pairwise disjoint open subsets of X such that for every F\in I,\,\exists U\in J such that F\subseteq U.

7.

Let D={ I:I is a discrete collection of closed subsets of X} and O=\{J:J is a collection of pairwise disjoint open subsets of X}. Then f:D\rightarrow O is a collectionwise normality operator on X if \forall I\in D, if f(I)=J then \forall F\in I,\,\exists U\in J such that F\subseteq U. N_{c}(X) denotes the set of collectionwise normality operators on X.

8.

X is effectively collectionwise normal if X is T_{2} and N_{c}(X)\neq \emptyset .

9.

X is highly separated if X is T_{2} and \{N_{c}(F):F\subseteq X\} has a choice function.

10.

X is functionally separated if for all pairs (A,\,B) of closed disjoint subsets of X there is a function f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] such that A\subseteq f^{-1}(0) and B\subseteq f^{-1}(1).

11.

X is Tietze-Urysohn if for every closed F\subseteq X and every continuous function f:F\rightarrow [0,\,1] there is a continuous function g:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] which extends f.

12.

Let C={ g:g:X\rightarrow [0, 1] and g is continuous}. A function f:E\rightarrow C is a Urysohn operator on X if \forall (A,\,B)\in E, if U=f(A,\,B) then A\subseteq U^{-1}(0) and B\subseteq U^{-1}(1). U(X) denotes the set of Urysohn operators on X.

13.

Let B=\{(F,\,U):F is a closed subset of X and U:F\rightarrow [0, 1] is continuous}. A function f:B\rightarrow C is a Tietze-Urysohn operator if \forall (F,\,U)\in B, if f(F,\, U)=V then V extends U.

14.

X is effectively functionally separated if U(X)\neq \emptyset . X is effectively Tietze-Urysohn if T-U(X) \neq \emptyset . (Where T-U(X) is the set of all Tietze-Urysohn operators on X.)

15.

X is highly functionally separated if \{U(A):A\subseteq X\} has a choice function.

16.

X is highly Tietze-Urysohn if {T-U(A):A\subseteq X\} has a choice function.

17.

X is collectionwise separated (or collectionwise Hausdorff) if it is T_{2} and for every discrete set I of singletons from X there is a set J of open subsets of X such that for every F\in I, there is a unique O\in J containing (the singleton) F.

Assume that (X,\,\leq ) is a linear order.

18.

A\subseteq X is convex if \forall (x,\,y)\in A^{2},\,\forall u\in X, if x<u<y then u\in A.

19.

(X, \leq ) is conditionally complete if each non-empty subset with an upper bound has a least upper bound and each non-empty subset with a lower bound has a greatest lower bound.

20.

(X,\,\leq ) is complete if X=\emptyset or every subset has a least upper bound and a greatest lower bound.

21.

Let X be a topological space, let E be defined as above and let \Omega (X) be the set of open subsets of X. A function f:E\rightarrow \Omega (X) is a monotone normality operator on X if for every (F,\,G)\in E the following conditions hold

(i)

F\subseteq f(F,\,G)\subseteq \overline{f(F,\,G)}\subseteq X-G.

(ii)

If (F^{\prime },\,G^{\prime })\in E,\,F\subseteq F^{\prime } and G^{\prime }\subseteq G then f(F,\,G)\subseteq f(F^{\prime },\,G^{\prime }).

22.

A topological space X is monotonely normal if it is T_{1} and there is a monotone normality operator on X.

23.

Let (X,\,\leq ) be a complete linear order and let E be the set of non-empty open intervals of X. An increasing choice function on (X,\,\leq ) is a function \ast :E\rightarrow X such that

(i)

\forall I\in E,\,\ast (I)\in I.

(ii)

If (a,\,b)\in E and (b,\,c)\in E then \ast ((a,\,b))\leq \ast ((a,\,c))\leq \ast ((b,\,c)).

24.

A topological space X is completely regular if for all open U\subseteq X and all p\in U, there is a continuous f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] such that f(p)=0 and \forall x\in X-U,\,f(x)=1.

25.

An ordered set (T,\,\leq ) is a lattice if any two elements have a greatest lower bound and a least upper bound. A lattice is bounded is it has a smallest and largest element.

26.

An ideal I in a lattice (T,\,\leq ) is prime if \forall x,\,y\in T, if x\wedge y\in I then either x\in I or y\in I.

27.

If T is a bounded distributive lattice a function f is a prime ideal choice function on T if for each proper ideal I of T,\,f(I) is a prime ideal containing I.

28.

Assume that T is a bounded distributive lattice in which every subset has a least upper bound then T is \vee -compact if for all F\subseteq T such that \bigvee F=1, there is a finite F^{\prime }\subseteq F such that \bigvee F^{\prime }=1. (If (\Omega ,\,\subseteq ) is the lattice of open sets of a topological space X then X is compact if and only if (\Omega ,\,\subseteq ) is \vee -compact.)

29.

Let E be a set. An ultra filter choice function f on E is a function such that for all proper filters I in \mathcal{P}(E), f(I) is an ultra filter containing I.

30.

Let E be a set and U an ultra filter on a set I. U is E-adequate if for every filter F in \mathcal{P}(E) there is a function g:I\rightarrow E such that g(U) contains F.

31.

A topological space is irreducible if it is not empty and is not the union of two proper closed subsets.

32.

A topological space X is sober if every closed irreducible subset of X is the closure of a unique singleton.

33.

A Banach algebra is a normed algebra in which every Cauchy filter converges.

34.

Let (I,\,\leq ) be a preorder (reflexive and transitive), let (E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I} be a family of sets and for each (\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I\times I let f_{\alpha ,\beta } be a function from E_{\beta } to E_{\alpha }. Assume that the f_{\alpha ,\beta } satisfy the following conditions:

(LP_{I})\ \alpha \leq \beta \leq \gamma \Rightarrow f_{\alpha ,\gamma }=f_{\alpha ,\beta }\circ f_{\beta ,\gamma }.

(LP_{II}) For all \alpha \in I,\,f_{\alpha ,\alpha } is the identity on E_{\alpha }.

Then ((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}) is called a projective system relative to the preorder (I,\,\leq ). Let E=\prod _{\alpha \in I}E_{\alpha } and for each pair (\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I\times I such that \alpha \leq \beta , let E_{\alpha ,\beta }=\{x\in E:f_{\alpha ,\beta }(x_{\beta })=x_{\alpha }\}. Then the set Y=\bigcap _{\alpha <\beta }E_{\alpha ,\beta } is called the projective limit of the projective system ((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}). Y is denoted \lim _{\leftarrow }(E_{\alpha },\,f_{\alpha ,\beta }). In case the preorder (I,\,\leq ) is directed to the right (that is, \forall (\alpha ,\,\beta )\in I^{2},\,\exists \gamma \in I such that \alpha \leq \gamma and \beta \leq \gamma .) we say that the projective system ((E_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\, (f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}) is directed.

35.

If ((X_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}) is a projective system relative to the preorder (I, \leq ) and if each X_{\alpha } has a topology C_{\alpha } such that f_{\alpha ,\beta } is continuous relative to the topologies C_{\alpha } and C_{\beta } then the system ((X_{\alpha })_{\alpha \in I},\,(f_{\alpha ,\beta })_{(\alpha ,\beta )\in I\times I}) is called a projective system of topological spaces. In this case the projective limit of the system with the topology induced by the product topology on \prod _{\alpha \in I}X_{\alpha } is called the the projective limit of the projective system of topological spaces.

36.

If (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a bounded, distributive lattice, X is a subset of A and F is a filter in A, then F respects X if X\subseteq F and \bigwedge X exists implies \bigwedge X\in F.

37.

If (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a bounded, distributive lattice, X is a subset of A and F is a filter in A, then F strongly respects X if X\subseteq F implies \exists y\in F such that \forall x\in X,\,y\leq x.

38.

If X is a subset of a bounded, distributive lattice (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) then X is of Boolean type if for all b\in A,\,[(\forall x\in X,\,b\vee x=1) and (\forall y\leq X,\,y\leq b)] implies b=1. (y\leq X means (\forall x\in X)(y\leq x).)

39.

If (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a bounded, distributive lattice we say that A has the Rasiowa-Sikorski property (respectively the strong Rasiowa-Sikorski property) if for all a,\,b\in A such that a\not \leq b and all sequences (X_{n})_{n\in \omega } of subsets of A of Boolean type there is a prime filter containing a, not containing b and respecting (respectively strongly respecting) each X_{n}.

40.

If (A,\,\wedge ,\,\vee ) is a bounded distributive lattice then an element a\in A is \vee -compact if for every subset I\subseteq A,\,\bigvee I=a implies (\exists J\subseteq I) (J finite and \bigvee J=a).

NOTE 72

We prove that form 207(\beta ) implies 209 for any ordinal \beta . (form 207(\beta ) is UT(\aleph _{\beta },\,\aleph _{\beta },\,<2^{\aleph _{\beta }}) and 209 is (\exists an ordinal \alpha ) (\forall X) (If X is a denumerable union of denumerable sets then \mathcal{P}(X) cannot be partitioned into \aleph _{\alpha } non-empty sets.)) Assume form 207(\beta ) is true. Then for any set X, if X is a denumerable union of denumerable sets, then |X|<2^{\aleph _{\beta }}. For any X which is the denumerable union of denumerable sets we have |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(X))|\leq |\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{P}(2^{\aleph _{\beta }}))|. NOTE 75

Several weak forms of AC are known to be equivalent to AC in ZF. These include:

1.

MC: The Axiom of Multiple Choice, form 67;

2.

LW: Every linearly ordered set can be well ordered, form 90;

3.

PW: The power set of a well ordered set can be well ordered, form 91;

4.

VB: Every vector space has a basis, form 66;

5.

A: The Antichain Principle, form 89; and

6.

C(LO,\,\infty ): Every linearly ordered family of non-empty sets has a choice function, form 202.

Consequently everything that implies one of these six forms is equivalent to AC in ZF. That is, 95, 109, 112, 114, 133, 147, 149, 164, 218, 264, 292, 333, 334, and 335(n) for n\geq 2, also imply AC in ZF. In fact in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} the following two chains of implications are provable: AC \rightarrow VB \rightarrow MC \rightarrow A \rightarrow LW \rightarrow PW, and AC \rightarrow C(LO,\,\infty )\rightarrow LW. With regard to the reverse implications, VB \rightarrow AC, MC \rightarrow VB and LW \rightarrow C(LO,\,\infty ) are open questions. The other reverse implications are known to be unprovable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. (See Jech [1973b], page 134, Felgner/Jech [1973], Blass [1984a], H. Rubin [1960], H. Rubin/J. Rubin [1985], Part I, 5, Brunner [1983a],[1984b],[1985a], Howard/Rubin [1977], Truss [1978], Keremedis [1996a],[1996], and note 18.) It follows from the two chains of implications that each of the twenty forms mentioned above implies PW, form 91, in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

In Pincus [1972], page 740, it is shown that if \neg \Phi is boundable (see Pincus [1972], p. 722 for the definition of boundable) and \Phi \rightarrow AC is a theorem of ZF, then \Phi \rightarrow form 91 (PW) is a theorem of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

NOTE 76

In this note we prove that form 126 (MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty )) implies forms 82 (If a set is infinite then its power set is Dedekind infinite.) and 185 (Every Dedekind finite, linearly ordered set is finite.)

It is clear from the lemma that MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) implies that the power set of an infinite set is Dedekind infinite. To show that MC(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) implies form 185, let X be a Dedekind finite set which is linearly ordered by \leq . The assumption that X is infinite leads to a contradiction as follows: By the lemma we get a sequence (Y_{n})_{n\in \omega } of finite subsets of X such that Y_{n}\subsetneq Y_{n+1} for all n\in \omega . If we define t_{n} to be the \leq -least element of Y_{n+1}-Y_{n} then (t_{n})_{n\in \omega } is an infinite sequence of distinct elements of X and therefore X is Dedekind infinite.

NOTE 81

We argue that form 30 (the ordering principle) implies form 83 (If every subset of \mathcal{P}(X) which is linearly ordered by \subseteq has a maximum element then X is finite.)

Assume X is infinite and let \leq be a linear ordering of X. There must be either a non-empty subset Y of X with no least element (under \leq ) or a non-empty subset with no greatest element. (If every non-empty subset of X has a least element then let x_{1} be the least element of X,\,x_{2} be the least element of X-\{x_{1}\}, etc. This produces a subset \{x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots \} with no greatest element.) If Y is an infinite subset of X with no greatest element, we get a linearly ordered subset A of \mathcal{P}(X) with no maximum by letting A=\{\{x:x\in Y\wedge x\leq y\}:y\in Y\}. We can proceed similarly if Y is an infinite subset of X with no smallest element.

NOTE 88

Either \mathcal{N}1 or \mathcal{N}3 may be used to prove that form 31 (UT(\aleph ^{0},\,\aleph ^{0},\,\aleph ^{0})) does not imply form 9 (Dedekind finite = finite). Form 9 is known to be false in these models and a proof that form 31 holds is given below. The result is transferable to ZF by Pincus [1972].

Let \mathcal{N} be either \mathcal{N}1 or \mathcal{N}3 with set of atoms A and \mathcal{G} the group of permutations used in defining the model. Assume that in \mathcal{N},\,B is a denumerable set of denumerable sets. Let e\subseteq A be a finite support for every b\in B. Such an e exists since B is well orderable in \mathcal{N}. Assume b\in B and x\in b. The proof will be completed by showing that e is a support of x. We argue by contradiction. Assume that e is not a support of x. We will show that under this assumption b has a subset of the same cardinality as an infinite subset of A which contradicts the countability of b.

Let e^{\prime }\supseteq e be a support of x. Then there is a t\in e^{\prime }\backslash e and a \phi \in \mathcal{G} which fixes e^{\prime }\backslash \{t\} pointwise and such that \phi (x)\neq x. (It follows that \phi (t)\neq t.) It can be verified that

\begin{equation*} \{\langle \psi (t),\psi (x)\rangle :\psi \in \mathcal{G}\ {\text{and}}\ \psi \ {\text{fixes}}\ e^{\prime }\backslash \{t\}\ {\text{pointwise}}\} \end{equation*}

is a one to one function from an infinite subset of A into b which is in \mathcal{N}.

NOTE 91

In this note we argue that form 269 is false in the first Fraenkel model \mathcal{N}1 of ZF^{0}. Form 269 is: “For every cardinal m, there is a set A such that 2^{|A|^{2}}\geq m and there is a choice function on the collection of 2 element subsets of A.” It suffices to show that for any set A in \mathcal{N}1 if the set [A]^{2} of two element subset of A has a choice function, then A is well orderable in \mathcal{N}1. Assume that A is such a set and assume that E is a (finite) support of A and a choice function f on [A]^{2}. Assume x\in A. We show by contradiction that E must be a support of x. Suppose not and let F be a support of x containing E. We claim there is a permutation \psi in \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E) and an element y\in A such that x\neq y,\,\psi (x)=y and \psi (y)=x. This would contradict our choice of E as a support for a choice function on [A]^{2} since \psi fixes \{x,\,y\} but moves both of its elements. To get such a \psi , let \phi \in \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E) satisfy \phi (x)\neq x and \phi moves only finitely many atoms. Assume F-E=\{t_{1},\,\ldots ,\,t_{n}\} and choose a set of atoms \{s_{1},\,\ldots ,\, s_{n}\} disjoint from F\cup \{t\in U:\phi (t)\neq t\}. Let \psi be the product of transpositions \prod _{i=1}^{n}(t_{i},\,s_{i}). The element \psi (x) is different from x since \phi (x)\neq x and \phi (\psi (x))=\psi (x). It is also clear that if y=\psi (x), then \psi (y)=x.

In this note we show that in \mathcal{N}23\,C(\infty ,\,2) (form 88) is false and C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) (form 126) is true. The proof that C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) is true is due to A. Rubin.

First we shall show that C(\infty ,\,2) is false. Let B be the set of subsets x of A such that the order type of x with respect to < is \omega . Let D be the set of equivalence classes of elements of B under the relation xRy iff the symmetric difference, (x-y) \cup (y-x) is finite. (Denote the equivalence class of x by [x].) Let P be the set of pairs of elements of D. P has no choice function in the model because if f is such a choice function and E\subseteq A is a support of f it follows that for all order preserving permutations \phi of A such that \phi fixes E pointwise and for all [x],\, [y] in D, if \phi fixes \{[x],\,[y]\} then \phi fixes both [x] and [y]. We can construct a \phi ,\,x and y for which this is false as follows: Since E is well ordered there are elements a,\,b\in A such that the interval (a,\,b) contains no points of E. Let \phi be an order preserving permutation of A that fixes E pointwise, fixes a and b but moves at least one element t of (a,\,b). We may assume (by replacing \phi with \phi ^{-1} if necessary) that t<\phi (t). Let x=\{\phi ^{2n}(t):n\in \omega \} and y=\{\phi ^{2n+1}(t):n\in \omega \}. Then \phi ([x])=[y] and \phi ([y])=[x] (and [x]\neq [y]).

Next, we shall show that C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ) is true in \mathcal{N}23. Let X=\{Y_{i}:i\in \omega \} be a denumerable set of non-empty sets in the model. Let B be a common support for X and the Y_{i}’s, i\in \omega . Let the open intervals of A-B be denoted by I_{\beta }, for \beta <\alpha . For each i\in \omega , choose (in the outer model) z_{i}\in Y_{i} and let B_{i} be a support of z_{i}. Let J_{\beta i}=I_{\beta }\cap B_{i}. (Note: Whenever we choose a sequence of elements in A, we choose them in increasing order. Also, \beta will range over \alpha , and i and j will range over \omega .)

We then define K_{\beta ji} as follows: For each \beta and i, choose E_{\beta i}=\{e_{\beta ji}:j\in \omega \} cofinal in I_{\beta } such that each e_{\beta oi}<J_{\beta i} and E_{\beta i}\cap \mathrm{cl}(B_{i})=\emptyset . Then define K_{\beta ji}= B_{i}\cap (e_{\beta ji},\,e_{\beta j+1i}). (If J_{\beta i} is not cofinal in I_{\beta }, choose E_{\beta i} such that e_{\beta oi}<J_{\beta i}<e_{\beta 1i} so there is only one non-empty K_{\beta ji}.)

For each \beta , choose \{c_{\beta i}:i\in \omega \} cofinal in I_{\beta } and choose \{d_{\beta ji}:i\in \omega \} in the interval (c_{\beta j},\,c_{\beta j+1}). For each \beta ,\,j, and i, let f_{\beta ji} be a function mapping K_{\beta ji} into the interval (d_{\beta ji},\,d_{\beta ji+1}) and let L_{\beta ji} be the range of f_{\beta ji}. Next, let f_{i} be an extension of \bigcup _{\beta ,j}f_{\beta ji} to a complete isomorphism of A fixing B. We claim that F=\{<Y_{i},\,f_{i}(z_{i})>:i\in \omega \} is a choice function for X that is in the model. Since f_{i} preserves B, we must have that f_{i}(z_{i})\in f(Y_{i})=Y_{i}. A support of F is \bigcup _{\beta ,j,i}L_{\beta ji} which is a well ordered union of the well ordered sets L_{\beta ji} and, therefore, can be well ordered.

The argument that form 43 (DC) implies [43 S] (If S is a relation on A such that (\forall x\in A)(\exists y\in A)(x\,S\,y) and x_{0} is any element of A, then there is a sequence a(1),a(2),\ldots of elements of A such that a(n)\,S\,a(n+1) for all n\in \omega and such that a(0)=x_{0}.) is as follows: Let S be a relation on a set A satisfying the hypotheses of [43 S] and assume that x_{0}\in A. NOTE 102

Form 289 (If S is a set of subsets of a countable set and S is closed under chain unions, then S has a \subseteq -maximal element.) is false in \mathcal{M}1. Let b be the generic set of generic reals in \mathcal{M}1, let E(b) be the set of all finite subsets of b, and let S=\{\cup x:x\in E(b)\}. Since b is generic, for any finite subset \{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\} of b,\,a_{0}\not \subseteq \cup \{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\} It follows that if x,\,y\in E(b), then \cup x\subseteq \cup y iff x\subseteq y. Hence, any chain in S corresponds to a chain in E(b) and a \subseteq -maximal element of S corresponds to a \subseteq -maximal element of E(b). We claim that there is no infinite chain in E(b). For suppose x_{0}\subset x_{1}\subset x_{2}\cdots is an infinite chain in E(b). Let a_{n} be the smallest element in x_{n+1}-x_{n} for n\in \omega . Then \{a_{n}:n\in \omega \} is a denumerable subset of b, which is impossible because b is Dedekind finite. Thus, all chains in E(b) are finite so E(b) is closed under chain unions. Consequently, S is closed under chain unions. Since b is infinite, E(b) has no \subseteq -maximal element and, therefore, S has no \subseteq -maximal element.

NOTE 106

This note contains results from McCarten [1988] and Schnare [1968] relating to forms [1 BF] (DT_{0}), [1 BG] (CT_{0}), [1 BH] (TT_{0}), and [1 BI] (MT_{0}).

[1 BF] (DT_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is dense in X. (Y is dense in X if there is no non-empty open subset O\subseteq X such that O\cap Y=\emptyset .)

[1 BG] (CT_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is codense in X. (Y is codense in X if there is no non-empty closed subset C\subseteq X such that C\cap Y=\emptyset .)

[1 BH] (TT_{0}): Every topological space X has a T_{0} subspace that is thick in X. (Y is thick in X if there is no non-empty open and closed (clopen) subset H\subseteq X such that H\cap Y=\emptyset .)

[1 BI] (MT_{0}): Every topological space has a maximal T_{0} subspace.

1.

Forms \mathrm{D}T_{0} and \mathrm{C}T_{0} are false if “T_{0}” is replaced by “T_{1}”. (A counter example is the topological space (\mathbb{R},\,\tau ), where \tau =\{G\subseteq \mathbb{R}:G=(a,\,\infty ), a\in \mathbb{R} \vee G= \emptyset \vee G=\mathbb{R}\}.) McCarten [1988].

2.

Form \mathrm{T}T_{0} remains equivalent to \mathrm{AC} if T_{0} is replaced by T_{n}, for any n such that T_{n} implies T_{0}. McCarten [1988].

3.

\mathrm{M}T_{0} is equivalent to \mathrm{M}T_{1}. Schnare [1968].

4.

Schnare [1968] shows that the statement \mathrm{MP} is false if \mathrm{P}=T_{2},\,T_{3},\,T_{4}, regular, completely regular, normal, paracompact, metrizable, linearly disconnected or discrete. (It follows from the lemma that if P is a property that is possessed by every finite discrete space, but not by a countably infinite minimal T_{1} space, then MP is false.)

NOTE 107

Good/Tree [1995] proves that each of [34 B] through [34 E] implies 34. In this note we supply the details of the converses.

In Kelley [1955], pages 173–2 there is an outline of a proof that form [34 B] (\omega _{1} with the order topology is not paracompact.) follows from \mathrm{AC}. We note that the proof requires only form 34 (\omega _{1} is regular.) and therefore 34 implies [34 B].

Let \mathcal{C} be the open cover of \omega _{1} from Kelley’s hint. That is, \mathcal{C}=\{\{\beta :\beta <\alpha \}:\alpha <\omega _{1}\}. We show that \mathcal{C} has no open, locally finite refinement by contradiction. Assume that \mathcal{A} is an open, locally finite refinement of \mathcal{C}. We define an increasing function f:\omega \rightarrow \omega _{1} by induction: f(0)=0. Assume that f(n) is defined. For each \beta \leq f(n), the set D_{\beta }=\{x\in \mathcal{A}:\beta \in x\} is finite since \mathcal{A} is locally finite. It’s also true that for each x\in D_{\beta },\, \sup \{\gamma :\gamma \in x\} is less that \omega _{1} since x is a subset of one of the elements of \mathcal{C}. Let g(\beta ) be the maximum of \{\sup (x):x\in D_{\beta }\}. g(\beta ) is also less than \omega _{1}. Now apply form 34 to the set W=\{g(\beta ):\beta \leq f(n)\}. This is a countable set of ordinals each <\omega _{1} and therefore \sup W<\omega _{1}. Let f(n+1) be the least ordinal greater than \sup W. The important property of the function f is that

\begin{equation*} (\forall n\in \omega )(\forall j<n)(\forall x\in \mathcal{A})(f(j)\in x\rightarrow f(n)\not \in x) \tag{$\ast $} \end{equation*}

The sequence \langle f(n)\rangle _{n\in \omega } is strictly increasing so its \sup (call the \sup \, \beta ) is a limit ordinal. Further, by form 34, \beta <\omega _{1}. Since \mathcal{A} is locally finite, there is an (open) neighborhood y of \beta such that \{x\in \mathcal{A}:x\cap \,y\neq \emptyset \} is finite. Since y is open and \beta is a limit ordinal, there is an ordinal \gamma <\beta such that the interval (\gamma ,\,\beta +1)\subseteq y. For some natural number k, this interval must contain f(n) for all n\geq k. For each n\geq k we consider the sets D_{f(n)}=\{x\in \mathcal{A}:f(n)\in x\}. These sets are pairwise disjoint (by (\ast )), each is non-empty and for each element x\in D_{f(n)},\, x\cap (\gamma ,\, \beta +1)\neq \emptyset . Therefore \{x\in \mathcal{C}:x\cap \,y\neq \emptyset \} is infinite, a contradiction.

To show that 34 implies [34 C] (\omega _{1} with the order topology has the property that every infinite subset has a limit point in \omega _{1}.), let X be an infinite subset of \omega _{1}. Since X is well ordered and infinite, it must have an initial segment of order type \omega . Form 34 implies that each such initial segment must be bounded, so the least upper bound of this set is a limit point of X in \omega _{1}.

If \omega _{1} is regular and contains a denumerable discrete family of open sets, then the set of smallest elements in each set would be an infinite set with no limit point, contradicting [34 C]. Thus, 34 implies [34 D] (\omega _{1} with the order topology does not contain a countable discrete family of open subsets.).

The uncountable open cover of \omega ,\,\mathcal{C}=\{\{\beta :\beta <\alpha \}:\alpha <\omega _{1} \}, described above does not contain a countable subcover. If it did we could construct a countable cofinal sequence in \omega _{1}, contradicting 34. Therefore, 34 implies [34 E] (\omega _{1} with the order topology is not Lindelöf.).

We give the proof that each pair of cardinal numbers has a greatest lower bound (glb) (form 187) is true in \mathcal{N}12(\aleph _{1}). (The proof is due to A. Rubin.)

Finally, if X \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\alpha _{q}\times q and Y \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\beta _{q}\times q are the representations of X and Y, we claim that Z= \bigcup _{q\in Q}\min (\alpha _{q},\,\beta _{q})\,\times \, q has the property that |Z|= \mathrm{glb}(|X|,\,|Y|). Clearly, |Z|\leq |X| and |Z|\leq |Y|. Suppose, |Z_{0}|\leq |X| and |Z_{0}|\leq |Y|. Also, suppose Z_{0} \approx \bigcup _{q\in Q}\gamma _{q}\times q is the representation of Z_{0}. By the lemma, \gamma _{q}\leq \alpha _{q} and \gamma _{q}\leq \beta _{q} for all q. Thus, \gamma _{q}\leq \min (\alpha _{q},\,\beta _{q}) for all q so it follows that |Z_{0}|\leq |Z|.

NOTE 110

In this note we prove the result from G. Moore [1982] that form 36 (If A\subseteq \mathbb{R}^{n} and A \bigcap B is countable for every bounded B then A is countable.) implies form 38 (\mathbb{R} is not the union of a countable family of countable sets.)

We prove the contrapositive. Assume that form 38 is false and therefore that \mathbb{R} = \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n} where each A_{n} is countable. Let f be any bijection between \mathbb{R} and the interval (0,1). For each n\in \omega let A_{n}^{\prime }=f^{\prime \prime }A_{n}+n (where for any set X of reals and any real t,\,X+t=\{x+t:x\in X\}). Then

(a)

A_{n}^{\prime }\subseteq (n,\,n+1)

(b)

|A_{n}^{\prime }|=|A_{n}| and therefore each A_{n} is countable.

(c)

There is an injection from \mathbb{R}= \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n} to \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n}^{\prime }(x\mapsto f(x)+n where n is the least natural number such that x\in A_{n}).

Let A= \bigcup _{n\in \omega }A_{n}^{\prime }. It follows from (a) that every bounded subset of A is contained in some finite union \bigcup _{n<N}A_{n}^{\prime }. Hence, by (b), every bounded subset of A is countable. By (c), A is uncountable hence form 36 is false.

Let X be an infinite \mathrm{T}_{2} topological space in \mathcal{N}1. We need to show that there is an infinite Y\subseteq X\ (Y\in \mathcal{N}1) such that Y has no infinite compact subsets (in \mathcal{N}1). If X is well orderable then it is clear that such a Y exists. Assume that X is not well orderable in \mathcal{N}1.

Choose an x\in X, a support E, an element a\in A, and a permutation \phi \in G which fixes E pointwise so that

(a)

E is a support of X and its topology.

(b)

E\cup \{a\} is a support of x and

(c)

\phi (x)\neq x. (And therefore by (b) \phi (a)\neq a.)

By the lemma, the set of pairs F=\{(\psi (x),\,\psi (a)):\psi \in G and \psi fixes E pointwise} is a one to one function (in the model \mathcal{N}1) from Y=_{\mathrm{def}}\{\psi (x):\psi \in G and \psi fixes E pointwise} onto A-E.

Since the topology on X is \mathrm{T}_{2} we can choose open sets C and D so that x\in C,\,\phi (x)\in D and C\cap D=\emptyset . Since Y can be put in a one to one correspondence with a subset of the atoms in the model, every subset of Y in the model must be finite or cofinite. This means that at least one of Y\cap C or Y\cap D is finite. We may assume that Y\cap C is finite by replacing C by C\cap \phi ^{-1}(D) if necessary. Under this assumption we can conclude that \mathcal{C}=\{\psi (C):\psi \in G and \psi fixes E pointwise} is an open cover for Y. Further each element of \mathcal{C} is finite. It follows that for any infinite subset Z of Y,\,\mathcal{C} is an open cover for Z without a finite subcover.

NOTE 117

Definitions from Cowen [1990] for forms [14 BD] through [14 BG]. A hypergraph is a pair H=\langle V,\, E\rangle where V is a set (of vertices) and E is a set of non-empty finite subsets of V. E is called the set of edges. H is finite if V is finite. K=\langle W,\, F\rangle is a subhypergraph of H=\langle V,\, E\rangle if W\subseteq V and F\subseteq E. W\subseteq V is independent in H=\langle V,\, E\rangle if no two elements of W belong to the same edge of H. W\subseteq V is a vertex cover of H=\langle V,\, E\rangle if each element of \mathrm{E} contains at least one element of W. An n-coloring of H=\langle V,\, E\rangle is a function f:V\rightarrow \{0,\,1,\,\ldots ,\,n-1\} such that |f^{\prime \prime }e|>1 for all e\in E with |e|>1.

NOTE 121

This note contains an argument that the order extension principle (form 49) together with “Every linear ordering has a cofinal well ordered subset.” (form 51) implies AC (form 1). This result was announced in Morris [1969].

Assume that Y is a set of non-empty sets. Let P be the set of choice functions f such that the domain of f is a subset of Y. We define the following partial ordering on P:

\begin{equation*} f\preceq _{0} g\Leftrightarrow \mathrm{dom}(f)\subsetneq \mathrm{dom}(g)\vee f=g. \end{equation*}

Extend \preceq _{0} to a linear ordering \preceq on P. Let \{f_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \beta \} be a cofinal subset of the linear ordering (P,\,\preceq ) where f_{\alpha }\prec f_{\gamma }\leftrightarrow \alpha \in \gamma . (\in is the usual well ordering on the ordinals.) The set W= \bigcup _{\alpha \in \beta } \mathrm{dom}(f_{\alpha }) has a choice function F defined by F(x)=f_{\alpha }(x) where \alpha is the least ordinal for which x\in \mathrm{dom}(f_{\alpha }). We complete the proof by showing that W=Y. If not, then there is some x\in Y-W. Let t be any element of x, then G=F\cup \{(x,\,t)\} is in P and has the property that \forall \alpha \in \beta ,\,f_{\alpha }\prec _{0}G and hence, since \preceq extends \preceq _{0},\,f_{\alpha }\prec G. This contradicts the cofinality of \{f_{\alpha }:\alpha \in \beta \}.

NOTE 122

In \mathcal{N}43, both C(\aleph _{0},2) (form 80) and the Multiple Choice Axiom (MC(\infty ,\,\infty ), form 67) are false.

C(\aleph _{0},2) is false in \mathcal{N}43: For each n\in \omega , let w_{n}=(a_{0}^{n},\,a_{1}^{n},\,\ldots ,\, a_{n}^{n}) be a fixed well ordering of P_{n}. (The function choosing these well orderings will not be in the model.) Let C_{0}^{n}={\phi (w_{n}):\phi is an even permutation of P_{n}} and C_{1}^{n}=\{\phi (w_{n}):\phi is an odd permutation of P_{n}}. Then for every n\in \omega , \{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\} is in \mathcal{N}43 and has empty support. In fact if \psi |P_{n} is even then \psi fixes \{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\} pointwise and if \psi |P_{n} is odd then \psi interchanges C_{0}^{n} and C_{1}^{n}.

If E is any support, then there is a \psi \in G that fixes E pointwise and an n\in \omega such that \psi |P_{n} is odd. Since such a \psi fixes \{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\} but moves both its elements, E is not a support of a choice function on \{\{C_{0}^{n},\,C_{1}^{n}\}:n\in \omega \}.

MC(\infty ,\,\infty ) is false in \mathcal{N}43: Let F be the set of all choice functions f:\omega \rightarrow A such that \forall n\in \omega ,\,f(n)\in P_{n}. Suppose that E is a support of a multiple choice function H on \mathcal{P}(F)-\{\emptyset \} in \mathcal{N}43. Let k= \sup \{|E\cap P_{n}|:n\in \omega \} and define T\subseteq F by T=\{f\in F:(\forall i>k)(f(i)\in P_{n}-E)\}. Since E is a support of T and of H,\, E is a support of H(T) which must be a finite, non-empty subset of T. Fix f in H(T) then for every g\in T for which g(i)=f(i) for i\leq k, there is a \phi \in G which fixes E pointwise such that \phi (f)=g. Therefore g\in H(T). Since there are infinitely many such g’s, H(T) is infinite. This is a contradiction.

NOTE 123

We shall prove that form 10 (C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0}))\ + form 163 (Every non-well orderable set has an infinite Dedekind finite subset.) implies form 231 (UT(WO,\,WO,\,WO)) and also that form 133 (Every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous set.) implies form 231. (It is shown in Brunner [1982a] that 10 + 163 implies 165 (C(WO,\,WO)).)

Suppose X is a well ordered set of pairwise disjoint well orderable sets. Assume Y=\bigcup X cannot be well ordered. Form 163 implies that Y has an infinite Dedekind finite set Z. Let T=\{w\cap \,z:w\in X\wedge w\cap z\neq \emptyset \} For each w\in Z,\,w\cap Z is a well ordered Dedekind finite set so it must be finite. If T is finite, then Z is a finite union of finite sets and is therefore finite. This contradicts the definition of Z. If T is infinite, then T is well ordered because X is well ordered. Therefore T must have a denumerable subset, U. U is a denumerable set of finite sets, so by 10, U has a choice set. This choice set is a denumerable subset of Z. This contradicts the definition of Z. Thus, the union of X can be well ordered.

Since form 133 (every set is either well orderable or has an infinite amorphous subset) implies form 10 (Brunner [1984b]) and 133 implies 163 (clear), it follows that 133 implies 231.

NOTE 124

A proof that form 314 (Every permutation on a non-empty set can be expressed as a product of two reflections.) implies form 119 (C(\aleph _{0},uniformly orderable with order type of the integers)).

Assume that B=\{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} is a denumerable set of denumerable sets and f is a function defined on \omega such that \forall i\in \omega ,\,f(i) is an ordering of A_{i} with order type that of the integers. We want to construct a choice function g for B so we may assume that the elements of B are pairwise disjoint.

Let \eta be the permutation of \bigcup B defined by \eta (a)= the immediate successor of a under the ordering f(A_{i}) where A_{i} is the unique element of B such that a\in A_{i}. By form 314, \eta is the product of two reflections: \eta =\phi \circ \psi .

Fix an i\in \omega and for each permutation \beta of \bigcup B, let \beta ^{\prime }=\beta \ |\ A_{i}. Then \eta ^{\prime }=\phi ^{\prime }\circ \psi ^{\prime } and \phi ^{\prime } and \psi ^{\prime } are reflections. We complete the proof by showing that exactly one of \phi ^{\prime } or \psi ^{\prime } has exactly one fixed point. (This fixed point will be g(A_{i}).)

Since \phi ^{\prime } and \psi ^{\prime } are both reflections, \phi ^{\prime } and \psi ^{\prime } can both be written as a product of disjoint cycles, \phi '=\prod _{i\in I}(s_{i},\,t_{i}) and \psi ^{\prime }=\prod _{j\in J}(c_{j},\,d_{j}). Assume that A_{i}=\{\ldots ,\,a_{-1},\,a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots \} where the elements are listed in the order determined by the ordering f(A_{i}). Then \eta ^{\prime } is the infinite cycle \eta ^{\prime }= (\ldots ,\,a_{-1},\, a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots ). Let r be the smallest positive integer such that for some integer k the transposition (a_{k},\,a_{k+r}) is one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}) or one of the (c_{j},\,d_{j})

We first show that r=1. Assume that r>1 and that (a_{k},\,a_{k+r}) is one of the (c_{j},\,b_{j}). (The argument is similar if (a_{k},\,a_{k+r}) is one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}).) This means that \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k})=a_{k+r}. Since \eta ^{\prime }(a_{k})=a_{k+1} (and r\neq 1), \phi ^{\prime }(a_{k+r}) must be a_{k+1}, hence the transposition (a_{k+1},\,a_{k+r}) must be one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}). This contradicts the definition of r.

Assume that (a_{k},\,a_{k+1}) is one of the (c_{j},\,d_{j}). (The argument is similar if (a_{k},\, a_{k+1}) is one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}).) This means that \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k})=a_{k+1}. Since \eta ^{\prime }(a_{k})= a_{k+1} we conclude that a_{k+1} must be a fixed point of \phi ^{\prime }. Further, since \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k+1})=a_{k} and \eta ^{\prime }(a_{k+1})=a_{k+2} we conclude that \phi ^{\prime }(a_{k})=a_{k+2}, that is, (a_{k},\,a_{k+2}) is one of the (s_{i},\,t_{i}). By this last conclusion, \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k+2})=a_{k}. It follows that \psi ^{\prime }(a_{k-1})=a_{k+2}, that is (a_{k-1},\, a_{k+2}) is one of the (c_{j},\,d_{j}). Continuing in this way, we see that for every natural number j,\,\psi ^{\prime } interchanges a_{k-j} and a_{k+j+1} and \phi ^{\prime } interchanges a_{k-j} and a_{k+j+2}. Therefore, \psi ^{\prime } has no fixed points and \phi ^{\prime } has exactly one fixed point.

NOTE 126

We give definitions for form [43 B] from Goldblatt [1985].

Let \Phi be a class of formulas in a language that includes the language of the sentential calculus and suppose the deducibility relation, \vdash , satisfies the following:

D1.

\emptyset \vdash \phi , for every tautology \phi .

D2.

\Gamma \cup \{\phi \}\vdash \psi iff \Gamma \vdash \phi \rightarrow \psi , where \Gamma \subseteq \Phi .

D3.

If \Gamma \vdash \phi and \Gamma \subseteq \Delta , then \Delta \vdash \phi , where \Gamma ,\, \Delta \subseteq \Phi .

NOTE 127

Forms [1 BZ] (Vector space multiple choice) and 346 (Vector space Kinna-Wagner principle) were suggested by K. Keremedis. It is clear that [1 BZ] implies 346. In this note we prove that 346 implies the Kinna-Wagner principle KW(\infty , < \aleph _{0}) (form [62 E]). Since the axiom of choice is implied by the conjunction of forms 62 and 67, we obtain a proof that 346+67 implies the axiom of choice. (Form 62 is C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}) and 67 is the axiom of multiple choice.) Similarly, since [1 BZ] implies form 67, we obtain the result: [1 BZ] implies the axiom of choice.

Let X=\{y_{i}:i\in K\} be a family of finite sets. For each y_{i} let U_{i} be the real vector space \mathbb{R}^{y_{i}} with pointwise addition and scalar multiplication. (If y_{i}= \{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\, a_{n}\} we could think of U_{i} as being the set of all formal sums k_{1}a_{1}+\cdots +k_{n}a_{n} where the k_{i}’s are real.) Let S_{i} be the subspace { g\in U_{i}:g is constant}. (Or in terms of formal sums, S_{i} is all formal sums ka_{1}+\cdots +ka_{n}.) Let V_{i} be the quotient space V_{i}=U_{i}/S_{i}. That is, V_{i} consists of all equivalence classes [g] of elements of U_{i} under the relation g\sim f\Leftrightarrow g-f\in S_{i}. By form 346 there is a family \{F_{i}:i\in K\} such that for each i\in K,\,F_{i} is an independent subset of V_{i}. Since U_{i} is finite dimensional F_{i} must be finite. Say F_{i}=\{b_{1},\,\ldots ,\,b_{r}\} then since F_{i} is independent, the element w_{i}=b_{1}+\cdots +b_{r} is not zero. The vector w_{i}=[g] for some g\in U_{i}. Assume f\in [g]. Then if a,\,a^{\prime }\in y_{i} and g(a)\leq g(a^{\prime }) it follows from the fact that f-g is constant that f(a)\leq f(a^{\prime }). Therefore the set K_{i}=\{a\in y_{i}:g(a) is minimum among the numbers g(a^{\prime }) for a^{\prime }\in y_{i}} is independent of the choice of g\in w_{i}. It is also true that K_{i}\neq y_{i}. This follows from the fact that w_{i}\neq 0 which implies that g is not constant. The family \{K_{i}:i\in K\} is therefore a Kinna-Wagner function for X.

NOTE 128

In this note we prove that in \mathcal{N}51, form 64 (There are no amorphous sets.) and form 90 (Every linearly orderable set is well orderable.) are true and form 221 (Every infinite set has a non-principal measure.) is false. The Hahn-Banach Theorem (form 52) implies 221, so it is also false. (See Brunner/Howard/Rubin [1996].)

We first note that for each finite ordered partition P= (B_{1},\,\ldots ,\,B_{n}) of A,\,G_{P}\in \mathcal{F}, where G_{P}=\{\psi \in G:\psi (P)=P\} and \mathcal{F} is the filter of subgroups which determine \mathcal{N}51. Further, if H\in \mathcal{F} then there is a finite ordered partition P of A such that G_{P}\subseteq H. Therefore for each x\in \mathcal{N}51, there is a finite ordered partition P of A such that (\forall \psi \in G_{P})(\psi (x)=x). We will refer to such a partition P as a support of x.

In order to prove that form 221 is false we shall give a proof that in \mathcal{N}51 there is no non-principal measure on A, the set of atoms.

Suppose, m is a non-principal measure on A supported by the partition P= (B_{1},\,\ldots ,\,B_{n}) of A. Since m is finitely additive on disjoint sets, m(A)=1, and m(\{a\})=0, for all a\in A. It follows that there must be an i\leq n such that B_{i} is infinite and m(B_{i})\neq 0. There exist pairwise disjoint infinite subsets, S_{1},\,S_{2}, and S_{3}, of B_{i} such that B_{i}=S_{1}\cup S_{2}\cup S_{3}. Suppose \sigma _{1},\,\sigma _{2}\in G_{P} are such that

1 \begin{equation} \sigma _{1}(S_{1})=S_{2}\cup S_{3}\ \mathrm{and}\ \sigma (S_{2}\cup S_{3})=S_{1} \cssId{texmlid179}{\tag{1}} \end{equation}

2\begin{equation} \sigma _{2}(S_{1})=S_{2},\,\sigma _{2}(S_{2})=S_{3},\ {\text{and}}\ \sigma _{2}(S_{3})=S_{1} \cssId{texmlid180}{\tag{2}} \end{equation} Then, we would have

(a)

m(S_{1})=m(S_{2}\cup S_{3})=m(S_{2})+m(S_{3}), by (1).

(b)

m(S_{1})=m(S_{2})=m(S_{3}), by (2).

Consequently, m(S_{1})=2m(S_{1}), which implies that m(S_{1})=0. Thus, by (b), m(B_{i})=0, which is a contradiction.

NOTE 130

In this note we prove that form [30 G] (Every \subseteq -chain in \mathcal{P}(X) is contained in a maximal \subseteq -chain) is equivalent to form 30 (The ordering principle). Form [30 G] was suggested by Adam Kolany.

Assume [30 G]. Let X be a set and let Y be a maximal \subseteq -chain in \mathcal{P}(X). Define \leq on X by a\leq b iff (\exists A\in Y)(a\in A\wedge b\not \in A). \leq is linear because if not there are a,\,b\in X such that a\not \leq b and b\not \leq a. If this happens then Y\cup \{A_{0}\} (where A_{0}=(\bigcup \{A\in Y:a\not \in A\})\cup \{b\}) is a chain in \mathcal{P}(X) which properly extends Y.

Assume form 30. Let X be a set and Y a \subseteq -chain in \mathcal{P}(X). Let \leq be a linear ordering of X. Define another linear ordering R on X by a\, R\,b iff [(\exists A\in Y)(a\in A\wedge b\not \in A)] or [(\forall A\in Y)(a\in A\leftrightarrow b\in A)\wedge a\leq b]. Then Y^{\prime }=\{A\subseteq X:(\forall a\in A)(\forall x\,R\,a)(x\in A)\} is a maximal \subseteq -chain containing Y.

NOTE 131

In this note we give a proof of form [ 0 AL] (For every set A, there is an \aleph which cannot be covered by fewer than |A| sets each of cardinality <|A|.) in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. Form [0 AL] was suggested by K. Keremedis.

Let A be a set and suppose that K is an aleph which is covered by fewer than |A| sets of cardinality <|A|. Let \leq be the usual ordering on K and let \bigcup _{b\in B}C_{b}=K where |B|<|A| and for each b\in B,\,|C_{b}|<|A|. Since each C_{b} is well orderable, |C_{b}|<H(A). (The function H is Hartogs’ aleph function, H(A) is the least aleph that is not \leq |A|.) Therefore the ordering (C_{b},\,\leq ) has order type that of an ordinal \alpha _{b}<H(A). Let f_{b} be the unique order automorphism from \alpha _{b} onto C_{b}. Let \gamma be a fixed element of K and define F:A\times H(A)\rightarrow K by F(b,\,\beta )=f_{b}(\beta ) if b\in B and \beta \in \alpha _{b} and F(b,\,\beta )=\gamma otherwise. F is onto and |K|=|\mathcal{E}| where \mathcal{E} is the set of equivalence classes \subseteq A\times H(A) under the relation q\sim r\Leftrightarrow F(q)=F(r). Therefore |K|=\aleph _{\sigma } where A\times H(A) has a partition of cardinality \aleph _{\sigma }. Therefore, if we let \aleph _{\rho } be the smallest well ordered cardinal greater than every cardinal in the set \{\aleph _{\sigma }:A\times H(A) has a partition of cardinality \aleph _{\sigma }}, then \aleph _{\rho } cannot be covered by fewer than |A| sets each of cardinality |A|.
