NOTE 133

In this note we prove that forms [1 F] and [1 CC] are equivalent to form 1.

Form [1 F] is “For all ordinals \alpha ,\,DC(\aleph _{\alpha }): Given a relation R such that for every subset Y of a set X with |Y|<\aleph _{\alpha }, there is and x\in X with Y\,R\,x, then there is a function f:\aleph _{\alpha }\rightarrow X such that \forall \beta <\aleph _{\alpha },\, \{f(\gamma ):\gamma <\beta \}\ R\ f(\beta ).)”. It is clear that form 1 implies [1 F]. To prove the converse, well order X by using Y\,R\,x\Leftrightarrow x\not \in Y and use DC(\aleph _{\alpha }) for sufficiently large \aleph _{\alpha }.

The question of the equivalence of [1 CC] and 1 was first raised by K. Keremedis. Form [1 CC] is the conjunction of PC(\aleph _{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty ): “Every denumerable family of odd sized (finite) sets has an infinite subfamily with a choice function.” and MC_{\omega ^{+}}: “For every natural number n\geq 1 and for every set of non-empty sets, there is a function f such that for each u\in x,\,f(u) is a non-empty finite subset of u such that |f(u)| and n are relatively prime.” We first prove that PC(\aleph _{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty ) implies “every denumerable family of odd sized sets has a choice function”. Let X=\{x_{n}:n\in \omega \} be a denumerable family of odd sized sets. For each n\in \omega , let y_{n}=\{f:f is a choice function for \{x_{i}:i\leq n\}}. |y_{n}|=|x_{1}|\cdots |x_{n}| and is therefore odd. Applying PC(\aleph _{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\,\infty ) to Y=\{y_{n}:n\in \omega \} gives an infinite subset Y^{\prime } of Y with a choice function F. Then defining G by G(x_{n})=F(y_{k})(x_{n}) where k is the least natural number \geq n for which y_{k}\in \mathrm{dom}(F) gives a choice function for X.

To prove that PC(\aleph _{0}, \mathrm{odd},\infty ) and MC_{\omega ^{+}} imply AC. It suffices to show that \forall n\in \omega ,\,C(\infty ,\,n)(form 61)+MC(form 67)+MC_{\omega ^{+}}+ “Every denumerable family of odd sized sets has a choice function” implies AC. This is because MC_{\omega ^{+}} is equivalent to \forall n\in \omega ,\, C(\infty ,\,n)+MC (by lemma 3 of Howard/A. Rubin/J. Rubin [1997]) and because PC(\aleph _{0},\,\mathrm{odd},\, \infty ) is equivalent to “Every denumerable of odd sized sets has a choice function”

Let X be a set of pairwise disjoint, non-empty sets. By MC there is an f:X\rightarrow \mathcal{P}(\bigcup X) such that \forall x\in X,\,\emptyset \neq f(x)\subseteq x and |f(x)| is finite. For each n\in \omega , let Y_{n}=\{x\in X:|f(x)|=n\}. By C(\infty ,\,n), Y_{n} has a choice function (even if Y_{n} happens to be empty, but it might be clearer to exclude n for which Y_{n} is empty). Therefore the set C_{n}=\{g:g is a choice function for Y_{n}} is non-empty. By MC_{\omega ^{+}} there is a function F defined on \omega such that F(n) is an odd sized subset of C_{n} for each n\in \omega . Since every denumerable of odd sized sets has a choice function, there is a function G defined on \omega such that for every n\in \omega ,\,G(n)\in F(n). We can now define a choice function Ch for X by Ch(x)=G(n)(x) where |f(x)|=n.

NOTE 134

In this note we prove the result from Luzin/Sierpiński [1917] that form 100 (If n and m are cardinal numbers, then m\leq ^{\ast }n\rightarrow \neg (n<m).) implies form 369 (If \mathbb{R} is partitioned into two sets, at least one has cardinality 2^{\aleph _{0}}.). We give a proof here because Luzin/Sierpiński [1917] is not readily available.

Since 2^{\aleph _{0}}=|\mathcal{P}(\omega )|=|2^{\omega }| it suffices to show that for any partition \{A,\,B\} of \mathcal{P}(\omega ), either |A|=|2^{\omega }| or |B|=|2^{\omega }|. Since |A|\leq |2^{\omega }| and |B|\leq |2^{\omega }|, by 100 it suffices to show that there is either a function from A onto 2^{\omega } or a function from B onto 2^{\omega }. Define f:\mathcal{P}(\omega )\rightarrow 2^{\omega } by the following: Assume X=\{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots \}\in \mathcal{P}(\omega ) where a_{0}<a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots . Then

\begin{equation*} (f(X))(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0 &\mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\ {\text{is even or}}\ |X|\leq n+1\\1 & \mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\ {\text{is odd}} \end{array}\right. . \end{equation*}

Assume that f|B is not onto 2^{\omega }. Then for some \gamma in 2^{\omega }, the non-empty set C= \{X\in \mathcal{P}(\omega ):f(X)=\gamma \}\subseteq A. Then we can define a function g from C onto 2^{\omega } as follows: Assume X=\{a_{0},\,a_{1},\,a_{2},\,\ldots \} \in C where a_{0}<a_{1}<a_{2}<\ldots and assume n\in \omega . If \gamma (n)=0, then a_{n+1}-a_{n} is even or |X|\leq n+1, and we define

\begin{equation*} (g(X))(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0 &\mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\equiv 0\mod 4\ {\text{or}}\ |X|\leq n+1\\1& {\text{if}}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\equiv 2\mod 4 \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}

If \gamma (n)=1, then a_{n+1}-a_{n} is odd and we define

\begin{equation*} (g(X))(n)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} 0& \mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\equiv 1\mod 4\\1& \mathrm{if}\ a_{n+1}-a_{n}\equiv 3\mod 4. \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}

The proof that g is onto 2^{\omega } could be done by induction, that is, given any \beta \in 2^{\omega } we could define by induction a sequence \langle a_{n}\rangle _{n\in \omega } so that X=\{a_{1},\,a_{2},\, \ldots \}\in C and g(X)=\beta .

NOTE 135

In this note we prove that form 18 (PUT(\aleph _{0},2,\,\aleph _{0})) and [18 B] (The union of a denumerable family of pairs has a denumerable subset.) are equivalent. It suffices to show that [18 A] (PC(\aleph _{0},2,\,\infty )) implies [18 B].

Let X be a denumerable family of pairs. By [18 A] there is a denumerable subset Y\subseteq X and a choice function f for Y. If the range of f is infinite then it is a denumerable subset of \bigcup X. If the range of f is finite, then for some t\in \bigcup X there are infinitely many elements y\in Y such that f(y)=t. Each such y has the form y=\{a_{y},\,t\}. In this case the set \{a_{y}:f(y)=t\} is a denumerable subset of \bigcup X.

NOTE 136

In this note we prove that the Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14) is true in \mathcal{N}19. We shall use Blass’ theorem (Blass [1986], Theorem 2) which characterizes Fraenkel-Mostowski models in which BPI is true. According to this theorem BPI holds in a Fraenkel-Mostowski model if and only if the model is determined by a filter of subgroups \Gamma with the Ramsey property described below.

Rado’s Corollary. Assume that n,p\in \omega and that \langle m_{i}\rangle _{i\in n}\in \omega ^{n}. Then there is a q\in \omega such that for all sequences \langle X_{i}\rangle _{i\in n} of disjoint sets such that |X_{i}|\geq q for every i\in n, if \Delta is a partition of \{Z\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}X_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap \,X_{i}|=m_{i})\} into two pieces there then is a sequence \langle Y_{i}\rangle _{i\in n} such that for all i\in n,\,Y_{i}\subset X_{i} and |Y_{i}|=p and \{Z\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}Y_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap \,Y_{i}|=m_{i})\} is a subset of one of the pieces.

Let F=\{\phi _{1}\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E),\ldots ,\,\phi _{k}\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\} be a finite subset of G/\mathrm{fix}_{G}(E). We will find a Y satisfying the condition from definition 1 above. We first note that it is easy to verify that

1 \begin{equation} (\forall \phi ,\,\psi \in G)(\phi \circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)=\psi \circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\Leftrightarrow \phi (E)=\psi (E)) \cssId{texmlid181}{\tag{1}} \end{equation}

Let E^{\prime }=\phi _{1}(E)\cup \cdots \cup \phi _{k}(E). E and E^{\prime } are finite and therefore there are natural numbers j_{0},\,\ldots ,\,j_{n-1} such that E\cup E^{\prime }\subseteq B_{j_{0}}\cup \cdots \cup B_{j_{n-1}}. For i\in n, define E_{i}=B_{j_{i}}\cap E,\,E_{i}^{\prime }=B_{j_{i}}\cap E^{\prime },\,m_{i}=|E_{i}| and let p= \max \{|E_{i}^{\prime }|:i\in n\}. The integers n,\,p and the sequence \langle m_{i}\rangle _{i\in n}\in \omega ^{n} satisfy the hypothesis of Rado’s corollary. Therefore there is a q\in \omega satisfying the conclusion. For i\in n, choose a set X_{i}\subseteq B_{j_{i}} so that |X_{i}|=q. Let Y= \{\phi \circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E):\phi (E)\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}X_{i}\}. We now show that this Y satisfies the condition of definition 1.

Let \Delta =\{\Delta _{1},\,\Delta _{2}\} be a partition of Y into two pieces. Let \Gamma _{1}=\{\phi (E):\phi \circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in \Delta _{1}\} and \Gamma _{2}=\{\phi (E):\phi \circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in \Delta _{2}\}. By (1), \Gamma =\{\Gamma _{1},\,\Gamma _{2}\} is a partition of \{Z\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}X_{i}:(\forall i\in n)\,|Z\cap \,X_{i}|=m_{i}\}. By Rado’s corollary, there is a sequence \langle Y_{i}\rangle _{i\in n} such that |Y_{i}|=p for i\in n and W= \{Z\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}Y_{i}:(\forall i\in n)(|Z\cap Y_{i}| =m_{i}\} is either a subset of \Gamma _{1} or a subset of \Gamma _{2}. We assume without loss of generality that W\subseteq \Gamma _{1}. Let \eta \in G be a permutation such that \eta (E_{i}^{\prime })\subseteq Y_{i} for i\in n. (This is possible since |Y_{i}|=p\geq |E_{i}^{\prime }|.) Then (since \phi _{t}(E_{i})\subseteq E_{i}^{\prime } for 1\leq t\leq k) \eta \phi _{t}(E_{i})\subseteq Y_{i} for i\in n and 1\leq t\leq k. Therefore, for 1\leq t\leq k,\, \eta \phi _{t}(E)\subseteq \bigcup _{i\in n}Y_{i}. Using this and the fact that |\eta \phi _{t}(E)\cap Y_{i}|=|\eta \phi _{t}(E_{i})|=|E_{i}|=m_{i} for 1\leq t\leq k and i\in n we conclude that \eta \phi _{t}(E)\in \Gamma _{1}. Hence \eta \phi _{t}\circ \mathrm{fix}_{G}(E)\in \Delta _{1}.

NOTE 137

We shall give a proof that [1 BU] (In every vector space over \mathbb{Q}, every generating set includes a basis.) implies 1, AC. Bleicher [1964] has shown that

[1 BU]implies C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}) (62), so it is sufficient to prove that [1 BU] implies MC (67). (The proof is due to K. Keremedis.)

Let X=\{x_{i}:i\in I\} be a set of pairwise disjoint infinite sets. For each i\in I, let V_{i} be the set of all functions from x_{i} to \mathbb{Q} such that for all f\in V_{i},\,\exists r\in \mathbb{Q} such that \{u\in x_{i}:f(u)\neq r\} is finite. Then V_{i} is a vector space. Let V be the weak direct product of the V_{i}’s. For each i\in I, define

\begin{gather*} G_{i}=\{F\in V\,:\,(\forall j)[(\forall u\in x_{j})(j\neq i\rightarrow F_{j}(u)=0)\wedge \\ (j=i\rightarrow (\exists u\in x_{j})(F_{j}(u)=1\wedge (\forall v\in x_{j})(v\neq u\rightarrow F_{j}(v)=0)\vee \\ (F_{j}(u)=0\wedge (\forall v\in x_{j})(v\neq u\rightarrow F_{j}(v)=1)))]\} \end{gather*}

Let G=\bigcup \{G_{i}:i\in I\}. Then G is a generating set for V. Let B\subseteq G be a basis for V. For each i\in I, let H^{i} be the function in V such that \forall u\in x_{j},

\begin{equation*} H^{i}(u)=\left\{\begin{array}{l} 0,\,j\neq i\\1,\,j=i \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}

For each i\in I,\,H^{i} can be uniquely represented as a linear combination of a finite number of basis elements. It follows from the definition of G_{i} that each basis element uniquely specifies an element in x_{i}. Thus, each H^{i} uniquely specifies a finite subset of x_{i}.

NOTE 138

In this note we include a proof due to K. Keremedis that form 375 (Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem) implies form 119 (C(\aleph _{0},uniformly orderable with order type of the integers).

Fix \mathcal{A}=\{A_{i}:i\in \omega \} as in form 19, where the A_{i} are pairwise disjoint. Let \bar{A}_{i}=\{a_{i}\}\cup A_{i}\cup \{b_{i}\}, where a_{i},\,b_{i} are chosen so that a_{i},\, b_{i}\not \in A_{i} and the \bar{A}_{i} are pairwise disjoint. Declare a_{i} to be less than every member of A_{i} and b_{i} to be greater than every member of A_{i}. Put X=\cup \{\bar{A}_{i}:i\in \omega \}. Order X by requiring: elements of \bar{A}_{i} are ordered in X the way they are ordered in \bar{A}_{i}, otherwise if x\in \bar{A}_{i} and y\in \bar{A}_{j} then x is less than y iff i<j. Put \bar{X}=X\cup \{a\},\,a\not \in X and declare a to be greater than every member of X. Clearly \bar{X} with the order topology is a compact \mathrm{T}_{2} space and consequently a \mathrm{T}_{4} space. Furthermore, G=A(=\{a_{i}: i\in \omega \})\cup B(=\{b_{i}:i\in \omega \})\cup \{a\} is a closed subset of \bar{X} and the function f:G\rightarrow [0,\,1] given by f(a)=0 and for i\in \omega \ f(a_{i})=1/(i+2), f(b_{i})=1/(i+1) is clearly continuous. Hence, f has a continuous extension \bar{f}: \bar{X}\rightarrow [0,1]. Put f_{i}=\bar{f}|\bar{A}_{i}. As \bar{f} is continuous it follows that f_{i} is also continuous. Since \bar{A}_{i} is compact it follows that f_{i} attains both its minimum and maximum values. We may assume that f_{i} attains its minimum at a_{i}, its maximum at b_{i} and, at every other point of A_{i}, it takes on values other than f_{i}(a_{i}) and f_{i}(b_{i}). Let C_{i}=f_{i}^{-1}((y_{i},\,1/(1+i))) where y_{i}= \frac{2i+3}{2(i+1)(i+2)} is the midpoint of the interval [1/(2+i),\,1/(1+i)]. Clearly C_{i}\neq \emptyset and by the completeness of \bar{A}_{i} and the continuity of f_{i} it follows that c_{i}= \inf (C_{i})\in A_{i}. Hence, c=\{c_{i}:i\in \omega \} is a choice set for \mathcal{A}, finishing the proof of the theorem.

NOTE 139

We give a proof that form 67 (MC, Multiple Choice Axiom) implies form 375 (Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem). To the best of our knowledge, this result is due to David Pincus.

Suppose X is a normal topological space. Then, if A and B are disjoint closed sets, there exist disjoint open sets C and D such that A\subseteq C and B\subseteq D. MC gives us a rule for choosing a finite number of pairs (C,\,D) with the above property. Since the intersection of a finite number of open sets is open, MC implies that there is a function F such that for each pair of disjoint closed sets (A,\,B), F(A,\,B)=(C,\,D), where C and D are disjoint open sets such that A\subseteq C and B\subseteq D. Thus, using the standard proof of Urysohn’s lemma (see, for example, Kelley [1955], p 115), there is a rule for choosing a function f:X\rightarrow [0,\,1] which is zero on A and one on B. Given this rule for choosing Urysohn’s function, the standard proof of the Tietze-Urysohn Extension Theorem can be given in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} (See, for example, Kelley [1955], p 242.).

NOTE 140

In this note we give a proof that form 214 (For every family A of infinite sets, there is a function f such that \forall y\in A,\,f(y)\subseteq y and |f(y)|=\aleph _{0}.) implies form 152 (Every non-well orderable set is the union of a pairwise disjoint, well orderable family of denumerable sets.)

Let X be a set which cannot be well ordered and let Y be the set of all infinite subsets of X. Form 214 implies that there is a function f such that for each y\in Y,\,f(y)\subseteq y and |f(y)|=\aleph _{0}. We define a function g on the ordinals so that g(0)=f(X) and g( \alpha )=f(X\,\backslash \, \bigcup _{\beta <\alpha }g(\beta )). Since X is a set, there is an ordinal \gamma such that X\, \backslash \, \bigcup _{\beta <\gamma }g(\beta ) is finite. We can use this function g to cover X with a well ordered family of pairwise disjoint denumerable sets.

NOTE 141

In this note we give the definitions for forms [1 CE] through [1 CH], [67 K] through [67 T], [126 G] through [126 K], 173, [173 A], 232, [232 A] through [232 G], 383, and [383 A] through [383 C].

NOTE 142

In this note we prove that form 234 (There is a non-Ramsey set.) implies form 282 (w\not \rightarrow (\omega )^{\omega }).

Assume that there is a non-Ramsey set A. The proof will be by contradiction. We therefore assume that \omega \rightarrow (\omega )^{\omega }. Then (using the definitions in note 97) for every F:\omega ^{\omega }\rightarrow \{0,1\} there is an infinite subset X of \omega such that either

(i)

(\forall g\in X^{\omega })(F(g)=0) or

(ii)

(\forall g\in X^{\omega })(F(g)=1).

Using A we define a function F:\omega ^{\omega }\rightarrow \{0,1\} by

\begin{equation*} F(g)=\left\{\begin{array}{l} 0\ \mbox{if}\ g\ \mbox{is strictly increasing and range}(g)\in A\\1\ \mbox{otherwise} \end{array}\right. \end{equation*}

Let X be the infinite subset of \omega guaranteed by \omega \rightarrow (\omega )^{\omega }. For each infinite subset Y of \omega , let g_{Y}\in \omega ^{\omega } be the unique strictly increasing function whose range is Y. Then F(g_{Y})=0 if and only if Y\in A. Either (i) or (ii) must be true of X and F. If (i) holds then for every infinite Y\subseteq X,\,g_{Y}\in X^{\omega } so F(g_{Y})=0 and hence Y\in A. On the other hand, if (ii) holds then for every infinite Y\subseteq X,\,g_{Y}\in X^{\omega } so F(g_{Y})=1 and hence Y\not \in A. This contradicts the assumption that A is non-Ramsey.

NOTE 143

Form [0 AM] is a form of the Hahn-Banach Theorem for separable vector spaces. We shall prove by induction that it is provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.

Assume V is a separable vector space, D=\{d_{0},\,d_{1},\,\cdots \} is a countable dense subset of V, and p:V\rightarrow \mathbb{R} satisfies p(x+y)\leq p(x)+p(y), and (\forall t\geq 0)(\forall x\in V)(p(tx)=tp(x)). Also assume that p satisfies the following condition:

\begin{equation*} (\forall \epsilon >0)(\forall x\in V-S)(\exists y\in D)\ \mbox{such that}\ (p(x-y)<\epsilon \ \mbox{and}\ p(y-x)<\epsilon . \tag{$\ast $} \end{equation*}

Let S be a subspace of V and let f be a linear function from S to \mathbb{R} such that for all x\in S,\,f(x)\leq p(x). We shall define by induction a countable set of linear functions G=\{g_{n}:n\in \omega \} such that g_{n}\subseteq g_{n+1} and such that the linear extension of f,\,f^{\ast }=\bigcup \, G, can be extended to all of V by using the condition (\ast ).

We define g_{0}=f. Suppose g_{n} has been defined and S_{n} is the domain of G_{n}. In what follows, we shall let d=d_{n+1} and g=g_{n+1}. If d is in the domain of g_{n}, then define g=g_{n}. Suppose that d is not in the domain of g_{n}. We would like to define g so that for any t\in \mathbb{R} and any x\in S_{n},\ g(td+x)=tg(d)+g(x)\leq p(td+x). Then tg(d)\leq p(td+x)-g(x). If t=1,\, g(d)\leq p(d+x)-g(x) and if t=-1,\,g(d)\geq g(x)-p(x-d). Let s= \sup _{x\in S}(g(x)-p(x-d)) and let i= \inf _{x\in S}(p(d+x)-g(x)). Then s\leq g(d)\leq i. Define g(d) to be the mid-point of the interval [s,\,i]. For any x\in S_{n}, We define g(x)=g_{n}(x) and, for each t\in \mathbb{R}, we define g(td+x)=tg(d)+g(x). Let f^{\ast }=\bigcup \{g_{n}:n\in \omega \}. It is clear that f^{\ast } is a linear function, f^{\ast }(x)\leq p(x) for all x in the domain of f^{\ast }, and D is a subset of the domain of f^{\ast }.

Let \epsilon >0 and x\in V. Then, by (\ast ), there is a y\in D such that p(x-y)<\epsilon and p(y-x)<\epsilon . If f^{\ast }(x-y)\geq 0, then 0\leq f^{\ast }(x-y)\leq p(x-y)<\epsilon . If f^{\ast }(x-y)<0, then 0<-f^{\ast }(x-y)=f^{\ast }(y-x)\leq p(y-x)<\epsilon . Consequently, |f^{\ast }(x-y)|<\epsilon and f^{\ast } can be extended to all of V.

NOTE 144

A proof that dependent choice (form 43) holds in FM models of \mathrm{ZF}^{0} in which the set of supports S is closed under countable unions. This includes models where S consists of all countable subsets of the set A of atoms.

Assume that \mathcal{N} is such a model and that R is a relation in \mathcal{N} such that for all x\in \mathrm{dom}(R) there is a y such that x\ R\ y. Then, in the ground model (where AC holds) there is a sequence (x_{n})_{n\in \omega } such that (\forall n\in \omega )(x_{n}\ R\ x_{n+1}). If for each n\in \omega ,\,x_{n} has support E_{n}, then \bigcup _{n\in \omega }E_{n} is a support for (x_{n})_{n\in \omega }. Hence, this sequence is in \mathcal{N}.

NOTE 145

A proof that form 287 (the Hahn-Banach theorem for separable normed linear spaces) implies form 222 (there is a non-principal measure on \omega ). This result and its proof are due to M. Morillon.

Let E be the vector space of bounded sequences of reals. Let M be a norm on E such that the normed vector space (E,\,M) is separable: for example, if x= (x_{k})_{k\in \mathbb{N}}\in E let M(x)= \sum \nolimits _{k\in \mathbb{N}}\frac{|x_{k}|}{(k+1)^{2}}. Here, the normed vector space (E,\,M) is separable because the set of sequences in \mathbb{Q}^{(\mathbb{N})} which end in an infinite sequence of zeros is dense in E.

For every x=(x_{k})_{k\in \mathbb{N}}\in E, let p(x)=\varlimsup \{x_{k};k\in \mathbb{N}\}. Hence, we obtain a sublinear functional p:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R}. Using form 287, let g:E\rightarrow \mathbb{R} be a linear functional such that g\leq p. We have p(1)=1 and p(-1)=-1. Hence, g(1)=1. For every finite subset A\subseteq \mathbb{N} we have p(1_{A})=p(-1_{A})=0, hence, g(1_{A})=0. Here 1_{A} denotes the characteristic function of the set A.

For every A\subseteq \mathbb{N}, lf m(A)=g(1_{A}), then m:\mathcal{P}(\omega )\rightarrow [0,\,1] is a non-principal measure on \omega .

NOTE 146

Form [43 W] is due to Claus-Peter Wirth. In this note we prove that it is equivalent to form 43. Form [43 W] is: Let M be a non-empty set partially ordered by < without <-minimal elements. Then there is a subset C of M which is linearly ordered by < such that C has no <-minimal element. Form 43 is the principle of dependent choice, DC. To prove [43 W] from DC let X=M and define R by x\,R\,y if and only if y<x. Then the sequence (x_{n})_{n\in \omega } which is guaranteed by DC is a linearly ordered subset of M with no <-minimal elements.

To prove [43 W] implies DC, let R be a relation on a set X such that \forall x\in X,\,\exists y\in X such that x\,R\,y. Let M be the set of all finite sequences (x_{1},\,x_{2},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}) of elements of X such that x_{1}\ R\ x_{2}\ R\ \ldots \ R\ x_{n} and define a relation < on M by (x_{1},\, \ldots ,\,x_{n})<(y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{m}) if and only if (x_{1},\,\ldots ,\,x_{n}) is a proper extension of (y_{1},\,\ldots ,\,y_{m}). M has no <-minimal elements so by (ii) there is a < chain C in M with no minimal element. From C an infinite sequence (x_{n})_{n\in \omega } can be constructed with the property that x_{n}\ R\,x_{n+1} for all n\in \omega .

NOTE 148

We give a proof that forms 154 and [154 A] are equivalent. First, it is clear that 154 implies [154 A]. To prove the converse, assume [154 A] holds. Let \{X_{i}:i\in \omega \} be a countable family of pairwise disjoint compact \mathrm{T}_{2} spaces and let Y be the one point compactification of \bigcup _{i\in \omega }X_{i}. Form [154 A] implies that Y^{\omega } is compact. Since \prod _{i\in \omega }X_{i} is a closed subspace of Y^{\omega }, it is also compact.

Part V References for Relationships Between Forms

Introduction

To explain this part of the book, it is helpful to consider some examples. Five typical lines are below.

The first two numbers are form numbers. The third number which occurs in parentheses is a code number for the status of the implication. For example, in the first line above, the number 3 means that the implication “form 43 implies form 63” is not provable in Zermelo-Fraenkel (ZF) set theory. The other code numbers that we use are

0

for “The status of the implication is unknown.”

1

for “The implication is provable.”

2

for “The implication is provable and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are 1.”

3

for “The implication is not provable in ZF.”

4

for “The implication is not provable in ZF and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are 1 or 3.”

5

for “The implication is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.”

6

for “The implication is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0} and this fact follows from implications whose code numbers are odd.”

7

for “The status of the implication is unknown and we have found the question asked somewhere in the literature.”

(See the introduction for the definition of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}.)

The implication codes are odd numbers for the most part. In a typical line following the code number, is a reference to a bibliography item and possibly a note and, in the case of a non-implication, a model number. (We normally only list one model even if there are several models with this property.) In the first example above, Felgner [1971a] refers to the Bibliography and M2 refers to the model \mathcal{M}2 of ZF from our models section. (\mathcal{M}2 is a model in which form 43 is true and form 63 is false.)

In the second example above we see that form 85 implies form 78 is not provable in ZF set theory; the reference is Brunner [1980]; and the model is the permutation model \mathcal{N}3. \mathcal{N}3 is a model of \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. However, many of the results obtained for permutation models can be transferred to ZF models because of the work of Jech/Sochor [1966a], [1966b], and Pincus [1971], [1972a], [1974c], [1977a]. If a result is transferable, the numeral 3 will occur in the line to mean that the implication is not provable in ZF set theory. Following the reference, we give the permutation model with a “\mathrm{T}” following its number to indicate the result is transferable. (See note 18 for a list of forms that are transferable and note 103 for a summary of the transfer results of Jech/Sochor [1966a] and [1966b] and Pincus [1971], [1972a], and [1977a].)

The letters “IC” following a model number indicate that an inaccessible cardinal was used to construct the model. In some cases, the reference is just a model. In these cases it is clear from the model itself why the implication does not hold. (See, for example, the line at position (317,3) and model \mathcal{N}38.)

It follows from example 3 above that form 67 implies form 80 is not provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}, the references are Fraenkel [1922] and Jech [1973b], and the permutation model is \mathcal{N}2. The last example above tells us that form 87 implies form 86 in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. The references are Jech [1973b] (p 120 theorem 8.1), Levy [1964], and additional information can be found in note 9 in the notes section of the book. When note 120 is the reference, we state which part of the note applies. For example, at position (152,67) the reference is note 120(41). This means that we are using item 41 in note 120 (67+122\leftrightarrow 1, where form 1 is AC) to obtain the independence result. Form 122 is true in \mathcal{N}15, so by note 120 part 41, form 67 must be false. (AC is false in all our models.) In addition, form 152 is true in this model. Consequently, there is a 5 at position (152,67) below.

If the reference is note 18, we mean that either the first form listed is true in every permutation (FM) model, the second form is false in each such model, or the second form is false in every Cohen model. We have several forms that depend on parameters. (See note 18 for a list of these forms.) Sometimes the relationships between such forms depend on the value of the parameters. For example, we have the following line below:

\begin{equation*} 120\qquad 33\qquad (0)\qquad \mathrm{note}15\ (\mathrm{see}\ \mathrm{M}47(n, M)) \end{equation*}

Both forms 120 and 33 depend upon parameters. The notation means that for certain values of the parameters, form 120 is true in the model M47(n, M) and form 33 is false. The reader should look at the model to determine when this holds.

Each of our weak forms of the Axiom of Choice is implied by AC (form 1), but for some of our forms, it is unknown whether they imply AC. Each one of these forms, n, is listed below in the form:

\begin{equation*} n\qquad 1\qquad (7)\qquad \mathrm{reference} \end{equation*}

Similarly, for some forms, it is unknown whether they are provable in \mathrm{ZF}^{0}. Each one of these forms, m, is listed below as:

\begin{equation*} 0\qquad m\qquad (7)\qquad \mathrm{reference} \end{equation*}

In these two cases, for those forms for which we have not found a reference in the literature we use “This project” as the reference.
